action. You requested that the City address these alleged violations within 1 S days of receipt of 
this letter. This letter and the accompanying enclosures serve as the City's response to the findings 
and requested actions in the NOV.

City of Lima 
Investigation of Sodium Hypochlorite Incident 
April 12-14, 2016 
Ineident: On April 14, 2016, it was discovered that approximately 2,500 gallons of Sodium Hypochlorite 
solution was missing from the south storage tank at the wastewater treatment plant. 
Investigative Process: The investigation process included interviews of all persons who may have had 
information regarding the incident, including plant operators on all three shifts, maintenance employees, a lab 
employee, a contractor and the plant assistant supervisor. Acdditionally, a tour was conduetecl of the storage 
tank area and the system for delivery of sodiurn hypochlorite to the plant. Documents reviewed included 
written reports by persons with information regarding the incident, the operator log for the period April 12 — 
April 22, 2016, the bili of lading for the shipment of 3,040 gallons of sodium hypochlorite solution, and the 
MSDS for the sodium hypochlorite, 
Discussion: Based on the shipping document and the testimony of the daytime operator, the City of Lima 
received about 3,040 gallons of Liquichlor (Sodium Hypochlorite solution 12.5%) between 11 AM and 
noon on April 12, 2016. The receiving operator indicated that the south tarik was filled completely, with 
excess allowed to flow to the :iorth tank. The operator also indicated that the outflow valve on both the 
north and south tanks was open upon his arrival. As part of preparation for receiving tl3e load of NaOCI in 
the south tank, the outflow valve on the north tank was closed. The south tank outflow valve was left open. 
Prior to the receipt of the NaOCI, the tank storage system had been tested for leaks iil accordance with 
standard operating practice. Additionally, the pumps used for rnetering NaOCI were not installed until 
April 15, 2016. The significanee of this fact is that the metering puinps act as an additional eontroi to the 
gravity flow of NaOCI to the chlorine contact tanks. With the south tank outlet valve open, the tank fuli, 
and no other valve having control over the system, the uncontrolled flow of approximately 2,500 gallons of 
sodiurn hypochlorite to the WWTP likely began after receipt of the shipment on April 12, 2016, and 
continued until the night operator closed the valve during his shift the following night. 
The testimony of the night shift operator supports this theory. On April 12, while collecting the 
composite sample, he did not not€ce a chlorine smell, but did observe the odor of chlorine on the following 
night (April 13-14) wlhile collecting the sample. He checked the incoming NaOCI line and found that no flow 
was going to the contact chambers. 1-le back-traced the line to the south storage tank where he found the 
outflow valve open, which he immediately closed. He attempted to identify the asnount of sodium hypochlorite 
in the south tank but was unable to do so in the darkness. He communicated this inforniation to the Assistant 
Superv'ssor the next inorning, April 14, The loss of NaOCi was discovered at about noon on April 14, 2016. 
The Plant Superintendent reported that he walked the river downstream of the WWTP on April 14 to deterzraine 
if an adverse 'smpact (fish kill) had occurred due to a discharge of sodium hypochlorite, but found no evidence 
of such.

text:
Cpnclusian: It appears that approxirnately 2,500 gallons of sodium hypochlorite discharged via gravity 
flow frorn the south tank through the disinfection system to the chlorine contact chambers over a period of 
approximately 36 hours; i.e., from the time the NaOCI was received at about noon on April 12, 2016, until 
the outflow valve on the south tank was closed on third shift the night of April 13-14, 2016.

text:
2. March 17, 2016 --- Lima received a Preliminary Compliance Review Eetter from OEPA 
indicating a weekly average limit violation for TSS at Station 604. 
3. March 18, 2016 --- Lima submitted a response Eetter to OEPA concerning the weekly average 
limit violation. 
4. April 25, 2016 --- Lima submitted a letter of explanation to OEPA concerning a potential 
accidental discharge of Sodium Hypochlorite from the WWTP on April 14, 2016. 
5. April 27, 2016 --- Lima received a Fact Sheet and NPDES Draft permit from OPEA for an initial 
14-day review. 
6. May 12, 2016 --- Lima submitted a follow-up letter to OEPA concerning the Sodium 
Hypochlorite discharge. 
7. May 23, 2016 --- Lima submitted a letter to OEPA containing its preliminary comments to the 
draft NPDES permit. 
8. June 1, 2016 --- Lima received an NOV letter from OEPA concerning the Sodium Hypochlorite 
discharge. 
9. June 6, 2016 --- Lima submitted a notification letter to OEPA informing of a daily maximum 
limit exceedance of Total Residual Chlorine at Station 001. 
10. June 10, 2016 --- Lima submitted a letter to OEPA requesting a change in the Operator of 
Record at the WWTP. 
11. June 15, 2016 --- Lima submitted a response letter to OEPA concerning the June 1 Sodium 
Hypochlorite NOV. 
Note: As to the June 1 Sodium Hypochlorite NOV, there was a subsequent letter from OEPA 
on July 11, and a response by the City on July 25. The NOV is now resolved. 
e. 	 A statement of any exceedances of NPDES permit limitations: 
Lima Progress Report: 
February, 2016 --- Lima's WWTP had an exceedance of the weekly average limit of 20 mg/I for 
Total Suspended Solids at Station 604. Lima recorded an average of 25.47 mg/! for the week 
of February 21-28, 2016, This exceedance was due to a significant rain event that occurred on 
2/24/16. The high flows from the rain event, in conjunction with the headworks construction 
currently underway at the plant, limited the capacity of the plant to process the suspended 
solids. 
2. June 6, 2016 --- Lima's WWTP had an exceedance of the daily maximum limit of 0.02 mg/I for 
Total Residual Chlorine at Station 001. Lima recorded 0.3 mg/l. This exceedance was due to 
inadequate adjustment of the chlorine feed rate as flows decreased following a rain event.

conditions in the mainline. The City continues to work with homeowners that experience 
chronic flooding on a case-by-case basis through a WIB Program that raises the lateral to a 
higher elevation and separates the storm water from the sanitary. Lima completed 3 WIB 
projects over the last six month period. Two additional project bids have been awarded and 
are expected to be completed in the next reporting period.

reported monthly to OEPA as part of the monthly Discharge Monitoring Report.

All of the 40 SSOs cited on the overflow report were directly related to rainfall events. In such 
events where the sewer system is stressed beyond capacity, city personnel manage the pump 
stations and WWTP via SCADA to maintain maximum treatment capability. The SSOs only

failure of equipment, a 24-hour emergency response crew is dispatched to address the situation.

title: edoc-472902.pdf
text:
Supplemental Environmentai Project, Ottawa River, Lima, Ohio 
1. Introduction 
The Federal Consent Decree (3:14-cv-02551-JZ) filed November 19, 2014, in the United States 
District Court Norther District of Ohio Western Division, requires the City of Lima to implement 
a Supplemental Environmental Project (SEP) to provide for the revitalization of the Ottawa 
River banks in Lima, Ohio. To implement the SEP and improve water quality and habitat along 
the study site (Ottawa River corridor), a riparian restoration plan was developed and 
implemented. The restoration focuses on ecological sustainability while adhering to the 
requirements SEP set forth in the Consent Decree so that the City can meet the requirement that 
"Lima shall maintain the plantings in good conditions through the life of the Consent Decree" 
(December 31, 2043). 
Geosyntec Consultants and Bassett and Associates collaborated with the City to create a 
sustainable restoration design for the Ottawa River corridoi•: an open woodland resembling an 
oak savanna. With EPA's approval, the Consent Decree schedule was adjusted from November 
30, 2015 to June 30, 2016 to allow for tree planting in the spring of 2016. The City also 
furthered ecological stewardship of the area, with established short-term and long-term 
maintenance plans. The selected restoration contractor, Davey Resource Group (Davey), is 
providing maintenance for a three-year period to provide control of invasive species and allow 
for native species to establish. Long-term maintenance will include mowing and prescribed 
ecological burns. 
2. Detailed Description of SEP 
The tasks outlined in the SEP included four items: ECOSystem Evaluation, Removing Large 
Trees, Clearing and Grubbing, and Planting. The schedule for tree planting was extended to 
Spring 2016 with EPA approval, for the benefit of oak species. The tasks were completed by the 
dates required under the Consent Decree: i.e. the ECOSystem Evaluation was completed by 
February 1, 2015, the removal of large trees by March 31, 2015, and clearing and grubbing tasks 
by August 30, 2015. As described below, continued monitoring of the SEP areas was conducted 
and follow up clearing or removals was performed as appropriate. 
2-1. Designated Areas 
Twenty (20) designated areas were delineated in the Consent Decree. The map of areas from the 
Consent Decree is attached in Appendix A. The SEP, as outlined in the Consent Decree, 
consisted of 6.6 acres of land along the Ottawa River, including 3,000 linear feet of stream bank 
on the north side of the river and 6,200 linear feet of stream bank on the south side of the river. 
The designated areas were expanded during the restoration to include an additional stretch of 
river bank on the north side of the river, which spanned 815 feet. More upland area was 
included, which increased the size of the area to 10.4 acres.

text:
Supplernental Environ►nental Project, Ottawa River, Liina, Ohio 
2-2. ECOSystem Evaluation 
The ECOSystem Evaluation occurred in the fall and winter of 2014 and was conducted by 
Bassett and Associates (Bassett). Dead, dying, diseased, and compromised trees were identified 
and are shown in Appendix B, ECOSystem Evaluation Map. Areas 8, 12, and 15 are not shown 
on the ECOSystem Evaluation Map. Areas 8, 12, and 15 were previously landscaped areas 
consisting of turf grass; no trees requiring removal were identified in these areas. 
The ECOSystem evaluation identified the most suitable restoration ecosystem and the 
undesirable species present. Undesirable tree species marked for removal included Chinese elm, 
black locust, honey locust, tree of heaven, and mulberry. Adventive (introduced but not fully 
naturalized) trees, including cottonwood and box elder, were also selected for removal. Green 
ash trees were removed in anticipation of the emerald ash borer. 
This task was completed on December 29, 2014, prior to deadline of February 1, 2015. 
Additionally, the restoration team has continually evaluated the plant life during the removal and 
treatment processes. After the large trees were removed in the spring of 2015, another evaluation 
was conducted in the summer of 2015. This evaluation identified some additional tree and shrubs 
which needed to be removed and also aggressive resprouts of invasive shrubs. 
2-3. Removal of Trees 
The dead, dying, diseased, and compromised trees identified in the ECOSystem Evaluation were 
removed by First Choice Tree by March 31, 2015. Fifty-three trees (greater than 12" in 
diameter) were removed, in addition to numerous small trees and shrubs. Treatment of invasive 
shrubs began in the fall of 2015, and additional removal of trees was conducted after September 
30, 2015 and completed in the fall of 2015. 
TAWA Tree Service conducted additional clearing and grubbing starting on April 20, 2015 and 
completed work on August 3, 2015. An additional ECOSystems evaluation was conducted July 
7 through August 10, 2015, which identified woody resprout regrowth and additional trees 
desired for removal. Davey mobilized on November 2, 2015 and began treating invasive species 
on November 3, 2015. A11 undesirable trees were removed from the site on February 13, 2016. 
2-4. Clearing and Grubbing 
Clearing and grubbing was complete prior to August 30, 2015. Invasive species removed 
primarily consisted of woody shrub species, such as honeysuckle and glossy buckthorn. Invasive 
herbaceous species, such as reed canary grass, Japanese knotweed, and garlic mustard, were also 
removed. 
Adventive and invasive species led to resprouts and regrowth, so follow-up clearing and 
grubbing was conducted in the fall to prepare for seeding of native grasses/wildflowers and 
planting of trees. All stumps were treated with a 20% solution of Garlon 4 in mineral oil

title: edoc-472902.pdf
text:
Supplemental Environtnental Project, Ottawa River, Lima, Ohio 
immediately following shrub removal. Foliar spraying was utilized to control invasive 
herbaceous growth. 
The restoration team also removed invasive herbaceous species and woody resprouts in the 
spring of 2016. Three additional invasive species trcatments are planned for the summer of 
2016, and will continue as needed until 2018. 
2-5. 	 Planting 
Planting for the Ottawa River riparian zone consisted of the tree stratum and three kinds of herb 
strata, as outlined below: 
® 	 Trees: 213 trees, primarily of oaks, were planted in the spring of 2016. Davey Resource 
Group provided and installed the trees. The tree planting plan is attached in Appendix C. 
Because oaks and hickories are most viable if planted in the spring, all trees were planted 
in early spring. Tree planting was completed the week of February 15, 2016. Planted 
tree species included: 
o Cercis Canadensis (CC) - Eastern redbud 
o Platanus occidentalis (PO) - Sycamore 
o Quercus alba (QA) - White oak 
o Quercus bicolor (QB) - Swamp white oak 
o Quercus ellipsoidalis (QE) - Northern pin oak 
o Quecus macrocarpa (QM) - Bur oak 
o Quecus rubus (QR) - Red oak 
Trees not only have aesthetic value to the local community, but help maintain the riparian 
ecosystem through water quality protection, soil stabilization, groundwater recharge, 
river shading, and aquatic habitat. The selected tree species, primarily oaks, are tolerant 
of and thrive in fire regimes. Oak trees, recommended in the planting plan, are nearly 
always dug in the spring time, and planted shortly after for survivability. 
Oak savanna seed mix: 6.6 acres of oak savanna seed mix was seeded in the spring of 
2016. Spence Nursery provided all seed mixes used for restoration. A map of seed mix 
areas is included in Appendix D. The majority of oak savanna seed mix was manually 
broadcasted due to the slopes of the river banks. The woodland savanna seed mix is 
included in Appendix E. 
o Prairie seed mix: 2.3 acres of prairie mix was seeded in the spring of 2016. Prairie seed 
was typically sown using a seed drill, unless slopes prevented that method. Where a seed 
drill could not be used, a disc harrow was used to rough up the seeding area. Seed was 
manually broadcasted in these areas and raked into achieve sufficient seed-soil contact.

3. 	 Problems Encountered 
The restoration team outlined the most sustainable approach for restoration (see Appendix G), 
which included short-term and long-term maintenance plans, and also identified the preferable 
tinling to plant oak trees. According to restoration professionals, oak trees have the greatest 
survivability if planted in the spring. A non-material consent decree modification was obtained 
to extend the completion date of the SEP from November 30, 2015 to June 30, 2016 to 
accommodate a spring tree planting. The spring planting and maintenance plans, including 
invasive species control, mowing, and prescribed burning, placed the installation of the SEP in 
line with sustainable restoration, with the goal of a restored ecosystem throughout the life of the 
Consent Decree (28 years). 
The SEP, as prescribed in the Consent Decree, did not include a maintenance plan. • Restoration 
industry standards require at least 3 to 5 years to establish a restored ecosystem. After the 
ecosystem is established, it must be maintained through the use of controlled burning or mowing. 
The City acquired Davey's services for at least 3 years (through October 31, 2018). Davey is 
required to achieve a controlled burn prior to leaving the site, at which point the City will be 
responsible for maintenance. The City is starting to budget for the cost of controlled burns. 
Geosyntec will provide a long-term maintenance plan. 
The SEP required 6.6 acres of restoration. The restoration plan developed by Geosyntec 
Consultants and Bassett and Associates included 10.6 acres of land, which specified a six-foot 
buffer along the river walk, The SEP did not include restoring the area between the river bank 
and the river walk. An additional pocket of invasive species was also identified. These areas 
were added to the restoration plan to help result in an overall plan that would be more conducive 
to long-terin management. 
After herbicide was applied to kill the turf grass in preparation for restoration to native prairie, it 
was noted by the City Parks representatives that additional buffer would be needed for the river 
walk to provide access for community recreational activities (organized runs, biking events, etc.). 
The buffer was increased along 2,500 linear feet between College Street and Main Street on the 
south side of the river, increasing the overall size of the buffer by approximately two-tenths of an 
acre in area. This includes an additional 3 feet of buffer and arcs around park benches. This had 
slight impacts on SEP areas 5, 6, 8a, 8b, 12a, 13, 17, and 19. Davey reseeded the damaged 
buffer area with new grass species. 
After the first pass of tree removal and clearing and grubbing, dense areas of the site previously 
inaccessible were evaluated for the presence of undesirable species. Select trees in the additional 
area addcd to the restoration (see Appendix D) and in the previously inaccessible areas were 
marked for removal. The trees were removed in the fall and winter of 2015. 
After planting, it was observed that the trees did not survive the planting. It is Davey Resource 
Group's assessment that environmental conditions (in other words wide fluctuations in 
temperature along with a possible late frost, followed by two periods of warm dry weather) may

The City of Lima has expended $494,122 to implement the SEP as of June 20, 2016. Additional

at $647,791.

6. Environmental and Public Health Benefits 
An i-Tree Hydro Analysis was completed in 2016 to quantify benefits resulting frorn the Ottawa 
River restoration. i-Tree Hydro (i-Tree) is a program developed by USDA Forest Service (2014) 
to simulate the effects of tree cover on xunoff and water quality. i-Tree was utilized to estimate 
the benefits of planting 213 trees as part of the SEP. Three alternative conditions were examined 
with i-Tree: 
• Baseline: The baseline condition represents the pre-restoratioii conditions. Additional 
conditions are compared to the baseline to quantify improvement.

As shown in Table 4 above, planting 213 trees as part of restoration has a quantitative benefit on 
water quality, especially with time. With the restoration, runoff is expected to decrease, along 
with associated pollutants. 
Although not provided in the i-Tree analysis, further restoration benefits relating to channel 
shading and streambank stabilization are also expected. The additional trees planted as part of 
the SEP constitute a public good that has the potential to benefit i•esidents of Lima for years to 
come (Wolf, 2007). Public health and well-being can be expected to increase as the River Walk 
continues to be enlianced. Trees provide improved air quality, and the clearing of invasive shrub 
species allows residents to enjoy the river recreationally, leading to improved mental health and 
increased use of the river walk for exercise activities, such as the upcoming 15 1h  Annual Freedom 
5K Run/Walk, held on July 4, 2016, or the Kewpee Triathlon/Duathlon on July 31, 2016, both of 
which will utilize the Ottawa River Walk as a portion of the course (www.ohiorunner.coln 
accessed 6/20/2016). 
Urban parks similar to what is being created in Lima, in part due to this SEP, can provide 
significant air quality benefits in urban areas. Trees can reduce urban heat islands and contribute 
to cooling effects in local neighborhoods increasing human comfort and reducing energy use and 
associated costs. The cooling effects provided by the tree canopy could lead to ancillary benefits 
such as reducing air pollution and reductions in ultraviolet radiation and carbon dioxide (Nowak 
and Heisler, 2010).

7. Conclusion 
Davey's restoration work will continue to October 31, 2018, a three-year restoration industry 
standard that will allow for intensive care of the area, including re-seeding, replanting, and 
continual invasive species control as necessary to establish a liealthy, native ecosystetn to be 
retained for the life of the SEP. A long-term management plan also will be developed to guide 
tlle City's efforts to maintain the restoratioii. 
Once native vegetation is fully established, the restoration area is intended to be maintained in 
the long-term using a regular schedule of prescribed fire. The resttltant landscape will resemble 
an oak savanna, with mixed tree species that are tolerant of, and thrive in, prescribed burn 
regimes. Tlie long-term use of prescribed fire also is an essential component to minimizing the 
return of invasive brush and weeds and rnaintaining a healthy understory of native grasses and 
forbs.

Subject: 	 Lima, Ohio Supplemental Environmental Project: Tree Planting Timeline 
To improve water quality and habitat along the Ottawa River corridor, a riparian restoration plan 
was developed. The restoration plan focuses on ecological sustainability while adhering to the 
requirements of the Supplemental Environmcntal Project (SEP) set forth in the Consent Decree. 
Those requirements include removing existing plant life and replanting with trees, grasses, and 
wildflowers by November 30, 2015 and the requirement that "Lima shall maintain the plantings 
in good conditions through the life of the Consent Decree" (December 31, 2043). However, in 
researching the most suitable tree species for the site, the restoration team identified that the 
timeline for the most desirable and sustainable restoration could not be feasibly completed in the 
duration specified in the SEP; instead tree planting needs to be extended into the Spring of 2016. 
This memo aims to outline the information that led the team to their conclusion. 
ELEMENTS OF RESTORATION 
The designed ecosystem is an open woodland resembling an oak savanna. Consistent with the 
requirements of the SEP, the restoration of the banks and riparian areas of the Ottawa River 
involves four principal elements: 
o 	 Clearing invasive and ecologically undesirable trees and brush; 
@ 	 Elimination of small woody/brush resprouts and saplings and elimination of invasive 
weeds and grasses; 
® 	 Establishment of a native wildflower and grass cover; and 
m 	 Planting of trees.

While clearing invasive trees is done in a relatively short timeframe, restoration is a long-term 
commitment. Invasive species are fast-growing, and have a large seed source on-site. Once the 
areas are cleared these seeds will likely sprout aggressively, and if not removed, will quickly 
overtake the areas that are being restored. Furthermore, native species may require multiple 
growing seasons to become fully established. As a result, restoration requires monitoring and 
adaptive management for at least 3 years, during which time additional invasive control, re-
seeding, and re-planting may occur. A cover crop will be used to help mitigate invasive species 
in early years while the native species are becoming establislied. 
Once native vegetation is fully established, the restoration area is intended to be maintained in 
the long-term using a regular schedule of prescribed fire. The resultant landscape will resemble 
an oak savanna, with mixed tree species that are tolerant of, and thrive in, prescribed burn 
regimes. The long-term use of prescribed fire also is an essential component to minimizing the 
return of invasive brush and weeds and maintaining a healthy understory of native grasses and 
forbs. 
TREE PLANTING 
An essential component of tlie SEP and the restoration plan is the planting of native tree species. 
Trees not only have aesthetic value to the local community, but help maintain the riparian 
ecosystem tlirough water quality protection, soil stabilization, groundwater recharge, river 
shading, and aquatic habitat. The restoration team selected which tree species would be most 
ecologically valuable to the restoration through the following means:

and thrive in fire regimes. Oak trees, and some of the related species (hickorics) that are

requirements of the Supplemental Environmental Project (SEP), These standards focus on the 
initial clearing, restoration, and tree and plant establishment phases over a recommended two to

an aesthetic, healthy, diverse community of primarily native vegetation to meet the objectives of 
water quality protection, soil stabilization, groundwater recharge, river shading, and aquatic 
habitat, consistent with the SEP.

elimination of itivasive weeds and grasses, and establishment of a native wildflower 
and grass cover. 
o Tree establislsment: planting overstory trees to meet the requirements of the SEP.

The parties to this action enter into this stipulation and file it in this case to document

for the Defendant, the City of Lima ("Lima"), to complete an Ottawa River bank planting and 
revitalization project that the Consent Decree requires as a Supplemental Environmental Project

frorn November 30, 2015, to June 30, 2016 — is appropriate because Lima's engineering 
consultants and landscape architects have advised that oak trees and hickoiy trees will be more

Tree Renioval 
The tree rentoval has been successfully completed according to the SEP plan. Other than

Seeding 
Davey Resource Group has completed two seeding passes for all sections of the SEP project

Species installed for the first seeding pass were consistent with those listed in the

(Solidago caesia), was not available in the trade and thus not included in the seed mix.

text:
For the secoiid seeding pass, a tiumber of gt•asses and sedges that were included in the first

fact that they were already planted in the first seeding pass, and were thus present in the seed

area were planted with the woodland seed mix per the SEP specifcations. 
SEP Seeding Assessmeatt 
Davey Resource Group completed the first of two vegetation monitoring site visits in early 
June to assess native plants that had stai-ted to germinate at the site. First year native seedings 
are typically fairly sparse and dominated by forbs rather than grasses. The initial assessment 
was conipleted by performing a ineander survey in each individual management unit of the 
SEP project area. All species observed werc noted, assigned an approximate aerial coverage 
within each management utiit, and were separated by vegetative community (ie. prairie 
versus woodland savanna areas). 
Due to the early growtlt stages of niost of the vegetation that is typically observed in the first 
tnonitoritig pass during the first growing season following seed installation, the first 
monitoring visit provides moi•e of a baseline assessment ofthe species currently growing and 
is not appropriate to determine the success of the first seeding pass or the viability of the 
seed mix as whole. During subsecluent visits to the project site, a number of natives species 
from the seed niixes were observed to be successfully germinating and in various stages of 
growth. Once the second monitoi•ing eveiit is completed in August, when more vegetation 
lias matured and a more complete cross section of the enierging and established vegetative 
community can be observed, the success of tlae wintei• 2016 prairie and savanna seeding 
passes can be better assessed. Seeded species observed during spring iiionitoring and 
subsequent site visits through the inonth of Juiie were iiiostly still in the i•osette stage of 
growth and often difficult to positively identify to the species, but through the end of June, 
seeded species that have been identified on the SEP pr•oject site are indicated in the tables 
iticluded in Attachrnent 1. 
Davey Resource Group recominends that it may be premature to indicate to the monitoring 
agencies tliat a remedial seeding plan is necessary or that the seeding has failed.. The first 
and second growing seasons followiiig a native seeding are typically tremendously different 
as far as what emerges. While Davey Resource Group planned for and recommetids

three months of growth following seeding are not indicative oi• representative of the success 
of the seeding. Late sumtner monitoring will provide additional important growtlf and

Supplenient Seeding Action Plan 
Gernaination Challenges 
While the overall success of the seeding is tiot assessed to be pi•oblematic at this time, 
notably tnissing fi•om the new growth in the seeding areas was a consistent presence of cover

Davey Resource Group will be perforining an overseeding of cover crop (annual oats and

Native seed germination has been liampered in some of the drill-seeded areas by thick niats 
of black medic (

text:
Africa. It is a comtnon weed in lawns, gardens, waste areas, roadsides, pastures, and 
cropland. Black medic is a low-growing, spreading annual or short-lived perennial 
(depending up climate conditions), that reproduces by seed and grows well in diy soil, soil 
low in nitrogen, compacted soil, and in sparse lawns. It is likely that the removal of the turf 
grass created favorable conditions for it to emerge this spring and quickly form dense nlats 
that are inliibititig the germination of the native seed in sotne of the SEP sections.. A positive 
aspect of black medic is that it produces nitrogen through an association witlt soil bacteria, 
and can provide benefits to the soils at the SEP site. That said, it is a problem at tlie site and 
needs to be addressed. 
The key to reducing black medic is preventing seed production. Small patches of it can be 
removed - ideally before seed production - by hand pulling when soils are moist, hoeing, 
tilling, or digging. Black medic growing in the SEP project site tends to be present in large 
patches and appears to be preventing any germination of the ttative seed or cover crop, so an 
appropriate approach at the SEP project site will be to till the areas and re-seed them. This 
should both break up the tnat of black inedic shading out the ground surface and aerate the 
soil sufficiently to nlake growth conditions less favorable for the black nredic and more 
favorable for the native seed and cover crop. Turning the black medic ittto the soil will also 
provide beneficial nutrients to assist witlt native plant germination. Black niedic does not 
thrive in the shade, so getting a solid cover crop established will also help reduce resurgence 
of the weed. If appropriate, topsoil may be placed and mixed into the soil where tilling is 
performed. 
For areas where germinatiou of hatid broadcast seed was poor, Davey Resource Group will 
place topsoil to help inerease germination. Sloped areas and rocky areas will be treated on an 
individual basis with consultation from the project designer. Areas of bare soil will be over 
seeded with a cover crop in late July/early August. Areas currently vegetated will not be 
overseeded with a cover crop this summer, unless the area is poorly vegetated due to the 
treatment of undesirable species. 
For supplemental seeding, Davey Resource Group will also plant the woodland savanna seed 
nlix around the trees as specified in the SEP. 
In addition, Davey Resout•ce Group will be performing selective mowing and cutting to help 
control weeds and tall growth along the SEP corridor after they have reached a height of 
approximately t2 inctles, generally every thirty days during the growing season. 
Replacer~rents and Seed Availabelity 
Prior to the second seeding pass, Davey Resource Group will obtain the list of available 
species from the native seed nut'sery aird coordinate with the project designer for approval of 
any potential substitutions that need to be made due to the lack of availability of any species

It is standard practice for native seed nurseries to reach out to their competitors in an attempt 
to obtain species of seed that they do not have available in tlteir own nurseries. When the 
term "not available in the trade" is used, it means that the tiurseiy has completed this

Tree Planting 
Instal lation 
Davey Resource Group cotnpleted installation of 213 balled and burlapped trees per the SEP 
plan. Planting locations were individually decided upon within each section of the SEP 
project area with the project Landscape Architect. Installation of the trees occurred during 
the dorrnant season. 
Spring I,ttspeetion 
During spring tree inspectioiis, the last of which occurt•ed in late May during monitoring 
visits, many of the trees - sycantores, redbuds, and pin oaks in particular, were starting to leaf 
out, but inconsistently. Typically by late May most of the trees should have been almost fully 
leafed out. Other trees species that were planted were not leafing ottt, btit still had gt'een

Davey Resource Group, the Davey Tree Nursery, and the City of f.inia, almost all of the 
trees that had started to leaf out had died, and the trees that had green twigs in late May were 
also dead. Tree naortality was estimated'at 100% and the dead trees were immediately

Mortality 
In the June 24, 2016, n}emo entitled "Tree Removal, Seeding, and Tree Planting," it was 
indicated that a prelinninary review of weather data froin the date of the tree planting was 
somewhat inconclusive and did not point otit any obvious weather event that inay have 
turned out to be a single "kill" event, and Davey Resotirce Group was awaiting additional

Additional infortnation regarding rainfall amounts and tetnperature trends was gathered in 
ot•der to assess the tree rnortality (please see the NOAA data for the City of Linia taken at the 
Lima Wastewater Treatnrent Platit in Attachment 1). In addition, quality of stock, tree 
transport, installation mcthods, and post-installation inaintenance were assessed, 
The following assessnient regarding the tree mortality must be read with the understanding 
that providing a single definitive catisal factor for the total loss ofthe tree plantings may not 
be feasible, but an assessrnetit of a combittation of factors rnay provide a comprehensive 
explanatiott behind the loss of the trees and help with planning the replacement of the trees. 
The total loss of an entire tree plantiiig is an tinprecedented event for the Davey coinpanies, 
and trying to understand why the trees died is extreniely important iii helping to insure the 
sticcess of the warranty plantings, which will be conipleted at no cost to the City of Lima. 
Tree Ti•ansporl 
'I'rees were transported to the project site on two 48-foot drop-deck tractor trailers and were 
covered with shade tarps. The tarps protected trees from wind scald, dehydration, possible 
road salt. This transport method is standard practice and has been used to transport trees for 
many successftil projects. It is Davey's assesstnent that the nfethod of transport did not 
contribute to tree mortality. 
I'ree Stock Quality 
The Davey Nursety provided quality stock of appropriate size according to the project 
specifications. The recomntended caliper for the trees according to the project specificatioiis 
was adhered to and the project designer on site appt•oved the stock prior to installation. Tree 
caliper for balled atid burlapped trees is measured at 6 inches above grade for trees up to

4-ineh diameter and the stock met tire caliper requirements. All ti'ees were dormant at the 
time of planting and were dtig tising standard nurseiy practice and care. It is Davey's 
assessrnent that the quality of stock did not contribute to tree mortality. 
Ti•ee Iitstallation 
Other than the titning of planting, the trees were planted according to pi•oject specifications 
and it is Davey's assessmeiit that the method of planting did not contribute to tree mortakity. 
Prior to installation, Davey Resource Group and the Davey Nursery made a recotnmendation 
to the City that all trees specified in the plan could be planted in the spring, and that the 
Davey Nursety had experieiiced good results with planting both the oak species and the other 
deciduous species in the early spring. The City agreed to allow the trees to be planted in a 
single planting event, in early spring of 2016. Due to the warmer than usual winter, the 
Davey Nursery moved the planting date up to mid-February and tlie trees were installed

i3'eather Corrditrons 
As mentioned above, pinning down a single event that may have contributed to the loss of 
the trees may not be feasible, but a cotnprehensive understanding of a conibination of factors 
that may have led to tree mortality is certainly worth discussing. Additional information 
regarding rainfall aniounts and temperature trends was gathet•ed in an attempt to assess the 
tree mortality (Attachment 2). 
On the day of the tree installation, which started on February 19, 2016, the low temperature 
was 22 degrees and reached a high of 43 degrees. There were stiow flurries in the morning 
which tapered off as the tempei•ature rose above freezing. 
According to the NOAA weather data, there were multiple wide fluctuations in tenrperatures 
following installation that were hard on the already stressed tiewly planted trees. 
Temperatures immediately following installation quickly rose to the high 60s in the daytime, 
while still dropping below freezing at iiight. For example, the high on February 2! was 68F 
and gradually fell back to a high of 31`F on the 27th. Even though teniperatures were warm 
during this period, tire lows were still in the tnid 20s. This trend contiiiued througli May, 
when the trees sliould have been starting to leaf otit atid the danger of frost damage 
increased. The period of April 2tid through the 17th saw a long trend of highs that gradually 
climbed from the 40s and 50s at the beginning of the month, to the higli 70s by the middle of 
the inonth. Still dui -ing this period however, the lows renrainiifg consistently below freezing. 
Davey Resource Group made visits to the site on Marcla 8 and April 20. In March, the trees 
that were cliecked liad green twigs and small live btEds, and while each individual ti•ee was 
iiot cliecked, conditions oii site with soil and weather were appropriate for the year - root 
balls were not dty and no visible da3nage to the trees was observed. On April 20, the site 
overall was driet•, but tlie soil around the ti -ees was still nioist below grade. Rain was 
forecasted through the following week, atld the area received over two inches of rain during 
the following two weeks. A few trees were pushing leaves, but a delay in leaf out was not of 
concern at that point due to the stress that iiewly planted trees are subjected to. Davey 
Resource Group was on site on.Iune 2 and 3 perfortnitig spring vegetation mottitoring, and at 
that time a large number of the sycarnore trees were starting to leaf out, but matiy of the 
other lrees had few if any leaves on thern. While eaclf tree was not individually assessment

were either starting to leaf out or liad buds andlor green twigs, indicating that they were still 
alive. In additioii, the soil in the root balls was iiioist. At this time, it was decided that tree 
bags would need to be placed

text:
While the lack of fully leafed ottt trees in early June was of concern, it was Davey Resource 
Group's opinion that the to•ees had experienced a late frost that had either killed offthe first 
leaves or delayed leafing out altogether. The presence of new leaves, live buds, and live 
twigs, indicated that the trees were likely recovering from a potential late frost. Accot -ding to 
NOAA data and the Arboriculture - the I ►rtegrated Managenietat ofLandscape 7'r•ees, Shrubs, 
and Vities (4th Edition), there were at least three events well into the spring season that may 
have led to frost damage on the trees. According to Arboriculture, "frost can occur in clear 
calm conditions at 40 degrees and befow". The NOAA weatlier data supports that this 
occurred consistently through early April, and then again at least three times through the 
month of May, when the trees would have been actively lea#ing out. 
ln addition to widely fluctuating temperatut•es and the likelihood of frost stress following tree 
installatiotl, there was a period in from May 22 through Jtine 1 where temperatures were 
consistently above average and rainfall was below average. While the root balls of the trees 
were nzoist oii the day of spring nionitoring, it is possible that it was only due to recent i•ain 
whieh masked the dry down that had occurred in the week prior, and that the ta•ees had not 
yet shown signs of heat or dry conditions. When the dead trees were discovered dturing the 
June 17, site visit, a recent rain of 0.92 inch rnoistened the root balls, but again likely 
masked a prior hot dry period between June 7 and June 14, that may have been the final 
stressor that contributed to the niortatity of the trees. 
It is Davey Resource Group's assesstnent that environmental conditions; wide fluctuations in 
teniperature along with a possible late frost, followed by two pei•iods of warm dry weather, 
may have contributed to the rnortality of the already sensitive newly planted trees. 
Tree Corrective Action Plan 
The Davey Tree Nursery will replace 100% of the trees per the SEP plan in the late of fall of 
2016 and spring of 2017. The titning of the replants shall be according to the SEP 
specifications: 
Deciduous Trees, particularly oaks: March l to June I

In order to support healthy growth and survival potential, the trees will be dug with larger

will plant all the trees in the spring, after risk of frost, if the project team agrees that this inay

Because the replants will be installed within the growing seasons of 2016 and 2017, each tree 
will be thoroughly watered following install and Davey Resource Group will conrnience with

again at the beginning of the growing season (estimated as late February/early March for the

Previous Calendar half year "Progress Report Period" 7/ 1/18 to 12/31/18 
Paragraph 33 of the Lima Consent Decree "CD") states that, on January 31 and July 31 after the Effective 
Date and continuing on January 31 and July 31 of each year until termination of the CD, Lima shall submit 
to USEPA and Ohio EPA a progress report regarding the implementation of the requirements of this 
Decree in the previous calendar half year ("Progress Report"). 
The Lima Consent Decree (CD) became effective on January 13, 2015 such that this report will commence 
reporting as of that date. The lettered paragraphs below parallel the format of paragraph 33 of the CD. 
Initiatives that were underway on the effective date of the CD are reported under Section b of this report. 
A statement setting forth the deadlines and other terms that Lima is or was required to meet by 
this Consent Decree since the date of the last Progress Report, whether and to what extent Lima 
has met these requirements, and the reasons for any noncompliance: 
Lima Progress Report: 
(1) July 1, 2018 --- Lima was required to submit a WWTP Flow Maximization Plan. Lima 
submitted the plan on June 28, 2018. 
b. A general description of the projects and activities conducted during the reporting period to 
comply with the requirements of this Decree, and a projection of work to be performed pursuant 
to this Consent Decree during the next reporting period. Notification to USEPA and Ohio EPA of 
any anticipated delay shall not, by itself, excuse the delay: 
Lima Progress Report: Lima currently has the following contracts underway: 
1. Lima Wastewater Treatment Headworks Proiect  — Commenced construction on July 
1, 2015. Building and tank construction is complete. Activities planned over the next 
six months include a continuation of the seeding of the nitrification tower and 
performance testing of the tower for TSS and BOD removal. 
2. CMOM Plan  — Lima submitted a plan revision to USEPA on 7/31/18 that included 
changes requested by Mr. Todd Brown in an email dated 3/20/18. 
Asset Manaeement  — Contract documents were signed and a Notice-to-Proceed for 
the Phase 1 High Street/Jameson Avenue Sewer Rehabilitation Project was issued on 
7/17/18. Commencement of field activities occurred on 9/18/18. Progress to date 
has included dye-water testing of laterals and installation of the first manhole.

title: edoc-990795.pdf
text:
Progress over the next six months is expected to include the following: 
• Complete installation of a 10-inch PVC sanitary sewer and manholes on High 
Street between N. Rosedale and N. Jameson. 
• Begin HDPE lining of the 78-inch and 54-inch segmented block sewers. 
4. Supplemental Environmental Proiect (SEP)  --- Project is complete. Maintenance of 
the project area will continue with the possibility of a spring burning. 
5. Simmon's Field CSO EQ Basin  -- Progress to date includes the following: 
• Excavation of soil and rock to the base elevation of the tank. 
• Completion of the diversion structure and partial completion of the 96-inch 
diversion pipe. 
• Partial completion of the pump station wet well. 
• Completion of bridge over the Ottawa River for future force main. 
• Completion of rock anchor installation. 
• Partially completion of base slab. 
• Initial framing of wall structure. 
Progress over the next 6 months is expected to include the following: 
• Completion of base slab. 
• Continued construction of walls and interior support structures. 
• Continued construction of pump station wet well. 
• Continued construction of 96-inch diversion pipe. 
• See attached Gantt chart for more detailed activities.

period, and the actions taken to rectify the problems:

Water-in-Basement (WIB) Events --- Lima recorded one WIB occurrence during the reporting

up into a basement. The City continues to work with homeowners that experience chronic 
flooding on a case -by-case basis through a WIB Program that raises the lateral to a higher 
elevation and separates the storm water from the sanitary. Lima completed 3 WIB projects in 
this reporting period, bringing the total number of home projects completed to 144 since 
program inception.

In compliance with the provisions of the Federal Water Pollution Control Act, as amended (33 U.S.C. 
1251 et. seq., hereinafter referred to as the "Act"), and the Ohio Water Pollution Control Act (Ohio 
Revised Code Section 6111), 
City of Mansfield 
is authorized by the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency, hereinafter referred to as "Ohio EPA," to 
discharge from the Mansfield Wastewater Treatment Plant, located at 385 S. Illinois Ave, Mansfield, 
Ohio, Richland County, to  (River Mile 11.18) in accordance with the conditions specified in Parts I, II, 
III, IV, V, and VI of this permit. 
This permit is conditioned upon payment of applicable fees as required by Section 3745.11 of the Ohio 
Revised Code. 
This permit and the authorization to discharge shall expire at midnight on the expiration date shown 
above. In order to receive authorization to discharge beyond the above date of expiration, the permittee 
shall submit such information and forms as are required by the Ohio EPA no later than 180 days prior to 
the above date of expiration.

John Logue

a.  A sanitary sewer overflow is an overflow, spill, release, or diversion of wastewater from a sanitary sewer system. Although the above table indicates that the 
Measuring Frequency for Overflow Occurrence is 1/Month, the intent of that provision is to specify a reporting frequency for Overflow Occurrence, not a

sewer overflows that enter waters of the state, either directly or through a storm sewer or other conveyance, must be reported under this monitoring station.  
 
b.  For the purpose of counting occurrences, each location on the sanitary sewer system where there is an overflow, spill, release, or diversion of wastewater on a 
given day that enters waters of the state is counted as one occurrence. For example, if on a given day overflows occur from a manhole at one location and from a 
damaged pipe at another location and they both enter waters of the state, record two occurrences for that day. If overflows from both locations continue on the 
following day, record two occurrences for the following day. At the end of the month, total the daily occurrences and report this number on Day 1 of the DMR. If 
there are no overflows during the entire month, report "zero" (0).

the requirements for Part 9221 E. or part 9222 D., "Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewater" or EPA Method 1680 or 1681 in 40 CFR Part 
136. Analysis results shall be obtained prior to sewage sludge being removed from the treatment facility.

A. Toxicity Reduction Evaluation 
 
As soon as possible, the permittee shall attain compliance with new effluent limits for whole effluent 
toxicity. The permittee shall conduct a Toxicity Reduction Evaluation (TRE) evaluation as expeditiously 
as practicable, but not later than the dates in the following schedule:  
 
1. No later than three months after the effective date of this permit, the permittee shall initiate the TRE to 
attain compliance with new whole effluent toxicity limits. This evaluation shall include, but not be limited 
to the following activities:  
 
a. The acquisition of plant information, including a description of plant treatment processes, design and 
operating data, and discharges tributary to the outfall.  
 
b. The evaluation of plant and treatment plant operations as they relate to effluent toxicity. The evaluation 
shall involve a review of the adequacy and performance of all treatment unit processes. If source toxicity 
is known, immediate measures shall be taken to control the source. 
 
c. The evaluation of in-plant, influent and effluent toxic pollutants to identify specific toxicants 
contributing to the whole effluent toxicity, including pollutants flowing into the outfalls from off-site.  
 
d. The evaluation of sources of effluent toxicants/toxicity. This shall include an evaluation of the potential 
for identified pollutants to contribute to the effluent toxicity.  
 
e. The evaluation of treatment or toxicity source control measures.  
 
2. No later than April 1, 2026, the permittee shall submit to Ohio EPA Northwest District Office an 
interim report detailing the progress of the plant performance evaluation. This report shall include any 
biomonitoring results and other relevant information that has been obtained. 
 
3. No later than April 1, 2027, the permittee shall complete the plant performance evaluation and submit a 
final report to Ohio EPA Northwest District Office detailing the results and conclusions. The report 
should include recommendations for actions required to attain compliance with new limits for whole 
effluent toxicity, along with an implementation schedule which includes fixed dates for completing these 
actions. If necessary, a complete Permit-to-Install (PTI) application and approvable detail plans shall be 
submitted to Ohio EPA. (Event Code 34599) 
 
4.  No later than April 1, 2028, the permittee shall attain compliance with the WET effluent limits.  The

D. Sanitary Sewer Overflow (SSO) Reporting Requirements  
 
A sanitary sewer overflow is an overflow, spill, release, or diversion of wastewater from a sanitary sewer 
system. SSOs do not include wet weather discharges from combined sewer overflows specifically listed 
in Part II of this NPDES permit (if any). All SSOs are prohibited. 
 
1. Reporting for SSOs That Imminently and Substantially Endanger Human Health 
 
a) Immediate Notification 
 
You must notify Ohio EPA (1-800-282-9378) and the appropriate Board of Health (i.e., city or county) 
within 24 hours of learning of any SSO from your sewers or from your maintenance contract areas that 
may imminently and substantially endanger human health. The telephone report must identify the 
location, estimated volume and receiving water, if any, of the overflow. An SSO that may imminently and 
substantially endanger human health includes dry weather overflows, major line breaks, overflow events 
that result in fish kills or other significant harm, overflows that expose the general public to contact with 
raw sewage, and overflow events that occur in sensitive waters and high exposure areas such as protection 
areas for public drinking water intakes and waters where primary contact recreation occurs. 
 
b) Follow-Up Written Report 
 
Within 5 days of the time you become aware of any SSO that may imminently and substantially endanger 
human health, you must provide the appropriate Ohio EPA district office a written report that includes: 
 
(i) the estimated date and time when the overflow began and stopped or will be stopped (if known); 
(ii) the location of the SSO including an identification number or designation if one exists; 
(iii) the receiving water (if there is one); 
(iv) an estimate of the volume of the SSO (if known); 
(v) a description of the sewer system component from which the release occurred (e.g., manhole, 
constructed overflow pipe, crack in pipe); 
(vi) the cause or suspected cause of the overflow; 
(vii) steps taken or planned to reduce, eliminate, and prevent reoccurrence of the overflow and a schedule 
of major milestones for those steps; and 
(viii) steps taken or planned to mitigate the impact(s) of the overflow and a schedule of major milestones 
for those steps. 
 
An acceptable 5-day follow-up written report can be filled-in or downloaded from the Ohio EPA Division 
of Surface Water Permits Program Technical Assistance Web page at:  
https://epa.ohio.gov/divisions-and-offices/surface-water/guides-manuals/permits-program-technical-
assistance

J. Limits Below Quantification 
 
The parameters below have had effluent limitations established that are below the Ohio EPA 
Quantification Level (OEPA QL) for the approved analytical procedure promulgated at 40 CFR 136. 
OEPA QLs may be expressed as Practical Quantification Levels (PQL) or Minimum Levels (ML). 
Compliance with an effluent limit that is below the OEPA QL is determined in accordance with ORC 
Section 6111.13 and OAC Rule 3745-33-07(C). For maximum effluent limits, any value reported below 
the OEPA QL shall be considered in compliance with the effluent limit. For average effluent limits, 
compliance shall be determined by taking the arithmetic mean of values reported for a specified averaging 
period, using zero (0) for any value reported at a concentration less than the OEPA QL, and comparing 
that mean to the appropriate average effluent limit. An arithmetic mean that is less than or equal to the 
average effluent limit shall be considered in compliance with that limit. 
 
The permittee must utilize the lowest available detection method currently approved under 40 CFR Part 
136 for monitoring these parameters.

sampling of the effluent shall be after disinfection. Both samples shall be collected on the same day or, 
alternately, the effluent sample may be collected following the influent sample by approximately the 
retention time of the POTW. 
 
Sampling of sludge shall be representative of sludge removed to final disposal. A minimum of one grab 
sample shall be taken during actual sludge removal and disposal unless the POTW uses more than one 
disposal option. If multiple disposal options are used, the POTW shall collect a composite of grab 
samples from all disposal practices which are proportional to the annual flows to each type of disposal. 
 
b. The results of these samples must be submitted on Ohio EPA Form 4221 with the permittee's annual 
pretreatment report. Samples may be collected at any time during the 12 months preceding the due date of 
the annual report and may be used to fulfill other NPDES monitoring requirements where applicable. 
 
9. Enforcement 
 
The permittee shall investigate all instances of noncompliance with pretreatment standards and 
requirements and take timely, appropriate, and effective enforcement action to resolve the noncompliance 
in accordance with the permittee's approved enforcement response plan. 
 
On or prior to November 15th of each year, the permittee shall publish, in a newspaper of general 
circulation that provides meaningful public notice within the jurisdiction served by the permittee, a list of 
industrial users which, during the previous 12 months, have been in Significant Noncompliance [OAC 
3745-3-03(C)(2)(h)] with applicable pretreatment standards or requirements. 
 
10. Reporting 
All reports required under this section shall be submitted through Ohio EPA's eBusiness 
Center/STREAMS, Division of Surface Water NPDES Permit Applications services.  The Ohio EPA 
eBusiness Center can be found in the link: https://ebiz.epa.ohio.gov/login.html 
 
a. Quarterly Industrial User Violation Report 
 
On or prior to the 15th day of February, May, August, and November, the permittee shall report the 
industrial users that are in violation of applicable pretreatment standards during the previous quarter. The 
report shall be prepared in accordance with guidance provided by Ohio EPA and shall include a 
description of all industrial user violations and corrective actions taken to resolve the violations. 
 
b. Annual Pretreatment Report 
 
On or prior to November 15th of each year, the permittee shall submit an annual report on the 
effectiveness of the pretreatment program. The report shall be prepared in accordance with guidance 
provided by Ohio EPA and shall include, but not be limited to: a discussion of program effectiveness; an 
industrial user inventory; a description of the permittee's monitoring program; a description of any pass 
through or interference incidents; a copy of the annual publication of industries in Significant 
Noncompliance; and, priority pollutant monitoring results.

11. Record Keeping 
 
All records of pretreatment activities including, but not limited to, industrial inventory data, monitoring 
results, enforcement actions, and reports submitted by industrial users must be maintained for a minimum 
of three (3) years. This period of retention shall be extended during the course of any unresolved 
litigation. Records must be made available to Ohio EPA and U.S. EPA upon request. 
 
12. Program Modifications 
 
Any proposed modifications of the approved pretreatment program must be submitted to Ohio EPA for 
review, on forms available from Ohio EPA and consistent with guidance provided by Ohio EPA. If the 
modification is deemed to be substantial, prior approval must be obtained before implementation; 
otherwise, the modification is considered to be effective 45 days after the date of application. Substantial 
program modifications include, among other things, changes to the POTW's legal authority, industrial 
user control mechanisms, local limits, confidentiality procedures, or monitoring frequencies. 
 
U. Biomonitoring Program Requirements  
 
The permittee shall continue to implement an effluent biomonitoring program to determine the toxicity of 
the effluent from outfall 2PE00001001.  
 
General Requirements 
 
All toxicity testing conducted as required by this permit shall be done in accordance with "Reporting and 
Testing Guidance for Biomonitoring Required by the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency" 
(hereinafter, the "biomonitoring guidance"), Ohio EPA, July 1998 (or current revision). The Standard 
Operating Procedures (SOP) or verification of SOP submittal, as described in Section 1.B. of the 
biomonitoring guidance shall be submitted no later than three months after the effective date of this 
permit. If the laboratory performing the testing has modified its protocols, a new SOP is required. 
 
Testing Requirements 
 
1. Chronic Bioassays  
 
For the duration of the permit, the permittee shall conduct chronic toxicity tests, as specified in Part I,A, 
using water fleas (Ceriodaphnia dubia) and fathead minnows (Pimephales promelas) on effluent samples 
from outfall 2PE00001001. These tests shall be conducted as specified in Section 3 of the biomonitoring 
guidance. 
 
2. Acute Bioassays  
 
For the duration of the permit, the permittee shall conduct definitive acute toxicity tests, as specified in 
Part I,A, using water fleas (Ceriodaphnia dubia) and fathead minnows (Pimephales promelas) on effluent 
samples from outfall 2PE00001001. These tests shall be conducted as specified in Section 2 of the 
biomonitoring guidance. Acute toxicity tests need not be performed for months in which chronic toxicity 
tests are conducted. Acute endpoints, as described in Section 2.H. of the biomonitoring guidance, shall be 
derived from the chronic test.  
 
3. Testing of Ambient Water  
 
In conjunction with the acute and chronic toxicity tests, upstream control water shall be collected at a

PART III - GENERAL CONDITIONS 
 
1. DEFINITIONS 
 
"Daily discharge" means the discharge of a pollutant measured during a calendar day or any 24-hour 
period that reasonably represents the calendar day for purposes of sampling. For pollutants with 
limitations expressed in units of mass, the "daily discharge" is calculated as the total mass of the pollutant 
discharged over the day. For pollutants with limitations expressed in other units of measurement, the 
"daily discharge" is calculated as the average measurement of the pollutant over the day. 
 
"Average weekly" discharge limitation means the highest allowable average of "daily discharges'' over a 
calendar week, calculated as the sum of all "daily discharges'' measured during a calendar week divided 
by the number of "daily discharges'' measured during that week. Each of the following 7-day periods is 
defined as a calendar week: Week 1 is Days 1 - 7 of the month; Week 2 is Days 8 - 14; Week 3 is Days 15 
- 21; and Week 4 is Days 22 - 28. If the "daily discharge" on days 29, 30 or 31 exceeds the "average 
weekly" discharge limitation, Ohio EPA may elect to evaluate the last 7 days of the month as Week 4 
instead of Days 22 - 28. Compliance with fecal coliform bacteria or E. coli bacteria limitations shall be 
determined using the geometric mean. 
 
"Average monthly" discharge limitation means the highest allowable average of "daily discharges" over a 
calendar month, calculated as the sum of all "daily discharges" measured during a calendar month divided 
by the number of "daily discharges" measured during that month. Compliance with fecal coliform 
bacteria or E. coli bacteria  limitations shall be determined using the geometric mean. 
 
"85 percent removal" means the arithmetic mean of the values for effluent samples collected in a period 
of 30 consecutive days shall not exceed 15 percent of the arithmetic mean of the values for influent 
samples collected at approximately the same times during the same period. 
 
"Absolute Limitations" Compliance with limitations having descriptions of "shall not be less than," "nor 
greater than," "shall not exceed," "minimum," or "maximum" shall be determined from any single value 
for effluent samples and/or measurements collected. 
 
"Net concentration" shall mean the difference between the concentration of a given substance in a sample 
taken of the discharge and the concentration of the same substances in a sample taken at the intake which 
supplies water to the given process. For the purpose of this definition, samples that are taken to determine 
the net concentration shall always be 24-hour composite samples made up of at least six increments taken 
at regular intervals throughout the plant day. 
 
"Net Load" shall mean the difference between the load of a given substance as calculated from a sample 
taken of the discharge and the load of the same substance in a sample taken at the intake which supplies 
water to given process. For purposes of this definition, samples that are taken to determine the net loading 
shall always be 24-hour composite samples made up of at least six increments taken at regular intervals 
throughout the plant day. 
 
"MGD" means million gallons per day. 
 
"mg/l" means milligrams per liter. 
 
"ug/l" means micrograms per liter. 
 
"ng/l" means nanograms per liter.

"Reporting Code" is a five digit number used by the Ohio EPA in processing reported data. The reporting

"Severe property damage" means substantial physical damage to property, damage to the treatment 
facilities which would cause them to become inoperable, or substantial and permanent loss of natural 
resources which can reasonably be expected to occur in the absence of a bypass. Severe property damage 
does not mean economic loss caused by delays in production. 
 
"Upset" means an exceptional incident in which there is unintentional and temporary noncompliance with 
technology-based permit effluent limitations because of factors beyond the reasonable control of the 
permittee. An upset does not include noncompliance to the extent caused by operational error, improperly 
designed treatment facilities, inadequate treatment facilities, lack of preventive maintenance, or careless 
or improper operation. 
 
"Sewage sludge" means a solid, semi-solid, or liquid residue generated during the treatment of domestic 
sewage in a treatment works as defined in section 6111.01 of the Revised Code. "Sewage sludge" 
includes, but is not limited to, scum or solids removed in primary, secondary, or advanced wastewater 
treatment processes. "Sewage sludge" does not include ash generated during the firing of sewage sludge 
in a sewage sludge incinerator, grit and screenings generated during preliminary treatment of domestic 
sewage in a treatment works, animal manure, residue generated during treatment of animal manure, or 
domestic septage.

beneficial use.

the reported sludge weight generated in a calendar year (use the most recent calendar year data when the

2. GENERAL EFFLUENT LIMITATION 
 
The effluent shall, at all times, be free of substances: 
 
A. In amounts that will settle to form putrescent, or otherwise objectionable, sludge deposits; or that will 
adversely affect aquatic life or waterfowl; 
 
B. Of an oily, greasy, or surface-active nature, and of other floating debris, in amounts that will form 
noticeable accumulations of scum, foam, or sheen; 
 
C. In amounts that will alter the natural color or odor of the receiving water to such degree as to create a 
nuisance; 
 
D. In amounts that either singly or in combination with other substances are toxic to human, animal, or 
aquatic life; 
 
E. In amounts that are conducive to the growth of aquatic weeds or algae to the extent that such growth 
become inimical to more desirable forms of aquatic life, or create conditions that are unsightly, or 
constitute a nuisance in any other fashion; 
 
F. In amounts that will impair designated instream or downstream water uses. 
 
3. FACILITY OPERATION AND QUALITY CONTROL 
 
All wastewater treatment works shall be operated in a manner consistent with the following: 
 
A. At all times, the permittee shall maintain in good working order and operate as efficiently as possible 
all treatment or control facilities or systems installed or used by the permittee necessary to achieve 
compliance with the terms and conditions of this permit. Proper operation and maintenance also includes 
adequate laboratory controls and appropriate quality assurance procedures. This provision requires the 
operation of back-up or auxiliary facilities or similar systems which are installed by a permittee only 
when the operation is necessary to achieve compliance with conditions of the permit. 
 
B. The permittee shall effectively monitor the operation and efficiency of treatment and control facilities 
and the quantity and quality of the treated discharge. 
 
C. Maintenance of wastewater treatment works that results in degradation of effluent quality shall be 
scheduled during non-critical water quality periods and shall be carried out in a manner approved by Ohio 
EPA as specified in the Paragraph in the PART III entitled, "UNAUTHORIZED DISCHARGES".

reasonable engineering judgment to prevent a bypass which occurred during normal periods of equipment 
downtime or preventive maintenance; and

determines that it will meet the three conditions listed above in paragraph 11.C.1.

PART IV. STORMWATER CONTROL MEASURES AND POLLUTION PREVENTION PROGRAMS 
 
In Part IV and in Part VI, the term "minimize" means reduce and/or eliminate to the extent achievable 
using control measures (including best management practices) that are technologically available and 
economically practicable and achievable in light of best industry practice. 
 
A.     Control Measures 
 
You shall select, design, install, and implement control measures (including best management practices) 
to address the selection and design considerations in Part IV.B, and meet the control measures/best 
management practices in Part IV.C and any applicable numeric effluent limits in Part I.  The selection, 
design, installation, and implementation of these control measures shall be in accordance with good 
engineering practices and manufacturer's specifications.  Note that you may deviate from such 
manufacturer's specifications where you provide justification for such deviation and include 
documentation of your rationale in the part of your SWPPP that describes your control measures, 
consistent with Part IV.J.3.  If you find that your control measures are not achieving their intended effect 
of minimizing pollutant discharges, you shall modify these control measures as expeditiously as 
practicable.  Regulated stormwater discharges from your facility include stormwater run-on that 
commingles with stormwater discharges associated with industrial activity at your facility. 
 
B.     Control Measure Selection and Design Considerations 
 
 
You shall consider the following when selecting and designing control measures: 
 
1. Preventing stormwater from coming into contact with polluting materials is generally more effective, 
and less costly, than trying to remove pollutants from stormwater; 
 
2. Using control measures in combination is more effective than using control measures in isolation for 
minimizing pollutants in your stormwater discharge;   
 
3. Assessing the type and quantity of pollutants, including their potential to impact receiving water 
quality, is critical to designing effective control measures that will achieve the limits in this permit; 
 
4. Minimizing impervious areas at your facility and infiltrating runoff onsite (including bioretention cells, 
green roofs, and pervious pavement, among other approaches) can reduce runoff and improve 
groundwater recharge and stream base flows in local streams, although care shall be taken to avoid 
ground water contamination; 
 
5. Attenuating flow using open vegetated swales and natural depressions can reduce in-stream impacts of 
erosive flows; 
 
6. Conserving and/or restoring of riparian buffers will help protect streams from stormwater runoff and 
improve water quality; and 
 
7. Using treatment interceptors (e.g., swirl separators and sand filters) may be appropriate in some 
instances to minimize the discharge of pollutants.  
 
C.     Control Measures/Best Management Practices (BMPs)

inside or protecting them with storm resistant coverings (although significant enlargement of impervious

c. Exceptions to Quarterly Visual Assessments 
 
The following are exceptions to quarterly visual assessments: 
 
 Adverse Weather Conditions: When adverse weather conditions prevent the collection of 
samples during the quarter, you shall take a substitute sample during the next qualifying 
storm event. Documentation of the rationale for no visual assessment for the quarter shall be 
included with your SWPPP records.  Adverse conditions are those that are dangerous or 
create inaccessibility for personnel, such as local flooding, high winds, or electrical storms, or 
situations that otherwise make sampling impractical, such as drought or extended frozen 
conditions. 
 Areas Subject to Snow: In areas subject to snow, at least one quarterly visual assessment shall 
capture snowmelt discharge, as described in Part IV.E.2. 
 Substantially identical outfalls: If your facility has two or more outfalls that you believe 
discharge substantially identical effluents, as documented in your SWPPP, you may conduct 
quarterly visual assessments of the discharge at just one of the outfalls and report that the 
results also apply to the substantially identical outfall(s) provided that you perform visual 
assessments on a rotating basis of each substantially identical outfall throughout the period of 
your coverage under this permit.     If stormwater contamination is identified through visual

F.     Storm Water Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) 
 
A stormwater pollution prevention plan (SWPPP) shall be developed to address each outfall that 
discharges to waters of the state that contains stormwater associated with industrial activity.  Stormwater 
pollution prevention plans shall be prepared in accordance with good engineering practices.  The SWPPP 
shall identify potential sources of pollution which may reasonably be expected to affect the quality of 
stormwater discharges associated with industrial activity from the facility.  The SWPPP shall describe and 
ensure the implementation of practices which are to be used to reduce the pollutants in stormwater 
discharges associated with industrial activity at the facility and to assure compliance with the terms and 
conditions of this permit.  Facilities must implement the provisions of the stormwater pollution prevention 
plan required under this part as a condition of this permit. 
 
The SWPPP does not contain effluent limitations; the limitations or benchmarks are contained in Part  
I.  The SWPPP is intended to document the selection, design, and installation of control measures.  As 
distinct from the SWPPP, the documentation requirements are intended to document the implementation 
(including inspection, maintenance, monitoring, and corrective action) of the permit requirements.

PART VI.    DEFINITIONS AND ACRONYMS 
 
Action Area - all areas to be affected directly or indirectly by the stormwater discharges, allowable non-
stormwater discharges, and stormwater discharge-related activities, and not merely the immediate area 
involved in these discharges and activities. 
 
Best Management Practices (BMPs) - schedules of activities, practices (and prohibitions of practices), 
structures, vegetation, maintenance procedures, and other management practices to prevent or reduce the 
discharge of pollutants to surface waters of the State. BMPs also include treatment requirements, 
operating procedures, and practices to control plant site runoff, spillage or leaks, sludge or waste disposal, 
or drainage from raw material storage.  See 40 CFR 122.2. 
 
Co-located Industrial Activities - Any industrial activities, excluding your primary industrial activity(ies), 
located on-site that are defined by the stormwater regulations at 122.26(b)(14)(i)-(ix) and (xi). An activity 
at a facility is not considered co-located if the activity, when considered separately, does not meet the 
description of a category of industrial activity covered by the stormwater regulations or identified by the 
SIC code list in in the Industrial Multi-Sector General Permit OHR000007, Appendix D. 
 
Control Measure - refers to any BMP or other method (including effluent limitations) used to prevent or 
reduce the discharge of pollutants to surface waters of the State. 
Director - the Director of the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency (Ohio EPA). 
 
Discharge - when used without qualification, means the "discharge of a pollutant."  See 40 CFR 122.2. 
 
Discharge of a pollutant - any addition of any "pollutant" or combination of pollutants to "surface waters 
of the State" from any "point source", or any addition of any pollutant or combination of pollutants to the 
waters of the "contiguous zone" or the ocean from any point source other than a vessel or other floating 
craft which is being used as a means of transportation. This includes additions of pollutants into surface 
waters of the State from: surface runoff which is collected or channeled by man; discharges through 
pipes, sewers, or other conveyances, leading into privately owned treatment works.  See 40 CFR 122.2. 
 
Discharge-related activities - activities that cause, contribute to, or result in stormwater and allowable 
non-stormwater point source discharges, and measures such as the siting, construction and operation of 
BMPs to control, reduce, or prevent pollution in the discharges. 
 
Drought-stricken area - a period of below average water content in streams, reservoirs, ground-water 
aquifers, lakes and soils.  
 
U.S. EPA Approved or Established Total Maximum Daily Loads (TMDLs) - "U.S. EPA Approved 
TMDLs" are those that are developed by a State and approved by U.S. EPA.  "U.S. EPA Established 
TMDLs" are those that are developed by U.S. EPA. 
 
Existing Discharger - an operator applying for coverage under this permit for discharges authorized 
previously under an NPDES general or individual permit. 
 
Facility or Activity - any NPDES "point source" (including land or appurtenances thereto) that is subject 
to regulation under the NPDES program.  See 40 CFR 122.2. 
 
Federal Facility - any buildings, installations, structures, land, public works, equipment, aircraft, vessels, 
and other vehicles and property, owned by, or constructed or manufactured for the purpose of leasing to, 
the federal government.
