text:
Response 33: No VOC monitoring is required for the engines due to their limited VOC emissions. As 
part of the allowable NOx emission limits, the engines have a certified non-methane hydrocarbon 
emission rate that is comparable to VOC. 
Comment 34: What VOC monitoring is required for the storage tanks? Are VOC emission controls 
required on the storage tanks, and what specific compounds will be monitored? What specific vapor 
control systems will be installed and monitored during tanker truck fuel transfers to prevent volatile 
organic emissions? Are Stage II vapor recovery systems or equivalent controls required for all fuel 
transfers? How frequently will vapor control equipment be inspected and by whom? What are the 
permitted emissions limits, specifically during fuel delivery operations? 
Response 34: Most of the tanks at this facility are "belly tanks" that will sit directly below each 
engine and have a capacity of 1,000 to 6,000 gallons. The potential VOC emissions from the storage 
tanks are extremely small--0.41 tons per year combined for all storage tanks. As such, the storage 
tanks are considered de minimis and have no permitting requirements. 
Comment 35: How often will the cooling towers be running? What is the permitted PM2.5  discharge 
from cooling tower drift? 
Response 35: Permitted cooling tower PM10  and PM2.5 emissions are 0.11 tons and 0.04 tons per 
year, respectively, for each emissions unit, which equates to approximately 4.0 tons PM10 and 1.4 tons 
PM2.5  for all cooling towers combined. Although a high level of redundancy will be built into the 
cooling systems, at least some of the cooling towers will run continuously. 
Comment 36: A commenter suggested the record does not explain the basis for key assumptions for 
the cooling tower emissions, including drift loss rates or PM fractions, nor does it identify how these 
assumptions will be verified. 
Response 36: The method for calculating particulate emissions from cooling towers is well 
understood, as is the control efficiency from drift eliminators. The permittee provided detailed 
calculations as part of the permit application. The permit requires the units to employ high-efficiency 
drift eliminators, achieving a "drift loss" of 0.001 percent or less. The calculations in the compliance 
section of the permit provide the basis for the drift loss rates and specify the exact methodology for 
calculating the drift loss rates and emissions. The emissions from the cooling towers will be 
demonstrated using actual measurements of solids in the water and water usage rates. 
Comment 37: The draft PTI does not demonstrate compliance with OAC 3745-31-05(D)(2)(c), which 
requires "adequate and enforceable methods" for establishing compliance. The permit does not 
specify how the load will be measured, what instruments will be used, what data systems will be 
required, or how load classifications will be recorded. What criteria are used to determine whether 
the unit is operating above or below 25% load? 
Response 37: Ohio EPA agrees that the permit should include additional details on how engine load 
will be measured and recorded. The PTI has been changed to require that the company provide 
additional clarification on the identification of load ranges when the engine choice has been made. 
The Title V operating permit will subsequently include the additional parameters necessary to 
determine how the load range is identified and recorded. 
Comment 38: Once a permit is issued, can it be revised? When is a permit review mandated? Would 
the community be notified of any changes to the permit? 
Response 38: Permits can be revised when needed. Permits are revised for various reasons, 
including a proposed expansion, to ensure compliance. A review would be completed, and if 
necessary, a revised permit will be issued before any changes are made to the operation. Compliance 
issues may also require changes to the permit. All permitting actions are public noti

title: 4132514.pdf
text:
Comment 39: What dust suppression and fugitive emission controls are required during the 
construction phase? How is Ohio EPA monitoring the pre-construction activities identified in OAC 
3745-31-33? What are the projected PM2.5 and PM10 emissions during construction? How will diesel 
emissions from construction equipment be mitigated? 
Response 39: During construction, there are no specific requirements in the air permit for diesel 
emissions or dust. Emissions from construction operations are not required to be quantified or 
included in a permit. Although construction activities identified in OAC Rule 3745-31-33 are 
allowed during the initial permit process, construction companies must comply with the nuisance 
rules specified in OAC 3745-15-07. Ohio EPA representatives have observed the site in its current 
state and will continue to maintain a presence through all steps in the process. Members of the 
community are welcome to contact us with any questions or concerns regarding pre-construction 
activities. 
Comment 40: Will this facility be classified as a major source under Clean Air Act Title V permitting 
requirements? How do these requirements align with the requirements associated with the PTI? 
Response 40: Yes, Bistrozzi will be a major for Title V. Title V permitting requires major sources of 
air pollution to consolidate all air-related requirements into a single, comprehensive operating 
permit to help ensure compliance with all permit obligations at a given facility. Except for 
requirements specifically associated with the initial construction, all emission limitations, 
monitoring, and record-keeping requirements are transferred to the Title V permit. Title V permit 
applications must be submitted within 12 months of the commencement of operations. Prior to 
issuance of the Title V permit, the Title V application and existing PTI are reviewed to ensure the Title 
V permit meets all necessary requirements. 
Comment 41: What are the total projected annual emissions (NOx, PMz.,, PM10, VOCs, CO, and 
hazardous air pollutants)? What is the projected worst-case emissions scenario during extended 
power outages? 
Response 41: The facility is permitted to emit 235.62 tons of NOx, 96.06 tons of CO, approximately 
4.0 tons of PM1(), and 1.4 tons of PMz., annually. These annual limits effectively cover the facility's 
worst-case emissions and serve as the facility's worst-case emissions. No annual limits are 
established for VOCs or for particulate matter on the engines; however, both values at maximum 
operating rates would be less than 10 tons per year for all permitted units. SOZ and hazardous air 
pollutants (HAPs) emissions are both less than 1 ton per year for the entire facility. There is also a 
small quantity of emissions from the exempt sources at the facility. 
Comment 42: The monitoring planned for this facility tests for several sizes of particulate matter, 
but does not identify the matter. Isn't this important given different matter has varying health related 
issues? 
Response 42: Ohio EPA has no information suggesting any measurable amount of hazardous 
particulate matter, such as metals, associated with the operations of the cooling towers or diesel 
engines. 
Comment 43: One commenter requested that Ohio EPA require the permittee to submit the monthly 
records mandated in Permit Condition B.4.b.1. which detail the number of gallons of fuel used by 
emissions units P001 through P115 while operating. 
Response 43: The annual emission limitations are based on hours of operation at certain loads, not 
the number of gallons of fuel used. Ohio EPA can request a review of the operational records at any 
time. 
Comment 44: How was it determined that the data center can emit between 100 and 500 single 
pollutant emissions?

title: 4132514.pdf
text:
Response 44: The potential emissions from this facility are based on manufacturer data and federal 
guidance on operating hours. Ohio EPA reviewed and confirmed the accuracy of the calculations 
presented in the permit application, which were then used to establish the permit's annual limits. 
Comment 45: What is being done to mitigate electromagnetic fields (EMF) radiation coming from 
the facility? 
Response 45: The regulation of EMF radiation is outside the scope of this permit. Ohio Department 
of Health has a study on EMF and health. 
Comment 46: The proposed operational limits lack technical plausibility. The assertion that testing 
and maintenance for 115 individual generators can be consolidated in a manner consistent with the 
proposed annual hour restrictions is not supported by industry practice or independent verification. 
Response 46: Ohio EPA disagrees with this assertion. The U.S. EPA has reviewed and agreed with 
the proposed operational limits. The permitting approach has been used in other permits throughout 
the state for many years, including at data centers currently operating. 
Comment 47: The permit record does not appear to adequately address short-term emissions events 
associated with generator testing or emergency startup scenarios. 
Response 47: Ohio EPA disagrees. The permit lists the hourly emission rates for both low-load (<_ 
25%) and high-load events. The company is required to track which load condition each engine is 
operating under whenever an engine is running. Ohio EPA has the right to request that a company 
test and demonstrate that the manufacturer's emissions rates are met. 
Topic: Diesel Engine Emissions and Operations 
Comment 48: Commenters suggested that Best Available Technology (BAT) requirements in the 
draft PTI do not demonstrate compliance with OAC 3745-31-05(A)(3) because it does not include 
sufficient supporting analysis. Further, it was suggested that BAT for NOx could be more stringent, 
including technologies such as enhanced controls (e.g., Selective Catalytic Reduction [SCR] or diesel 
particulate filters), if not Tier 4 technology. What make and model, and emissions control technology 
are required for Tier 2 generators? 
Response 48: US EPA recently reviewed the federal regulations (40 CFR Part 60 Subpart IIII) and 
determined that the 2010 performance standards for emergency engines remain acceptable. No 
specific make, model, and emissions control technology is required for Tier 2 engines, but they must 
comply with all applicable state and federal rules. Tier 2 engines are designed and certified by the 
manufacturer to meet the emission limitations in 40 CFR Part 60 Subpart IIII. Additionally, as 
specified by rule, compliance with 40 CFR Part 63 Subpart ZZZZ is achieved through compliance with 
40 CFR Part 60 Subpart IIII. BAT requirements were reviewed and include compliance with all 
applicable federal rules as well as modeling for NOx. Applicable federal standards are the basis for 
the BAT determinations in this permit. 
Comment 49: One commenter indicated the Bistrozzi permit should require periodic testing on the 
engines like what is required in permits issued in Nebraska. 
Response 49: Ohio EPA has reviewed permits issued by the Nebraska Department of Water, Energy, 
and Environment that require engine testing. While emission rates can vary between similar sources, 
Ohio EPA does not believe this potential variability alone should trigger testing, especially since the 
engines may operate infrequently. Ohio EPA relies upon U.S. EPA certifications to set emission limits 
and assess compliance. By including "if required" in the permit's testing sections, Ohio EPA keeps the 
right to require testing if needed. Factors like engine age, how often and how long it's used, and 
results of visual inspections will be considered if testing is needed. For now, no testing is required 
through the PTI, although Ohio EPA retains the authority to conduct emissions tes

title: 4132514.pdf
text:
Comment 50: The draft PTI does not demonstrate that the anticipated operation of the facility will 
remain within the federal definition of "emergency operation:' What is the definition of "emergency" 
operation in the permit? What is the maximum permitted annual hours of operation for each 
generator, and how will compliance be verified? What are the real-time monitoring and public 
reporting requirements that will ensure generators are not operated beyond emergency use 
parameters? If generators are used for demand response or grid support (not just emergencies), does 
the permit cover those emissions? 
Response 50: 40 CFR Part 60 Subpart IIII does not define what constitutes an "emergency" but it 
does provide the following example: the production of "power for critical networks or equipment 
(including power supplied to portions of a facility) when electric power from the local utility (or the 
normal power source, if the facility runs on its own power production) is interrupted." 40 CFR Part 
60 Subpart IIII explicitly states what circumstances do not constitute an "emergency ; which includes 
maintenance, allowances to supply power to the grid to ensure reliability for the infrastructure, and 
peak shaving. 
Per 40 CFR Part 60 Subpart IIII, there is no limit on the use of emergency stationary internal 
combustion engines in emergency situations. However, regardless of the frequency or duration of 
electrical outages, the draft PTI does not allow the permittee to operate the engines for an unlimited 
number of hours, as the emissions from all operating scenarios count toward existing permit limits. 
40 CFR 60.4211(f) establishes the parameters that must be met for an engine to be considered an 
emergency stationary internal combustion engine (ICE), including a 100-hour limitation on 
operating hours in non-emergency situations. Federal regulation 40 CFR 60.4211(f)(3) establishes 
specific parameters under which the engines can use a 50-hour allowance to supply power to the 
grid to ensure reliability to the infrastructure. Peak shaving, when not done as specified in 40 CFR 
60.4211(f) (3), but strictly as a financial arrangement, is prohibited. 
Term C.1.b)(2)c. of the draft permit explicitly states that the proposed sources must operate within 
compliance of "40 CFR 60.4211(f) in order to be considered an emergency stationary ICE under Part 
60, Subpart IIII:' 
The permit has the necessary recordkeeping and reporting requirements in place to track operating 
hours and the type of operation that occurred. The engines have non-resettable hour meters that are 
checked by Ohio EPA personnel during inspections. If an engine no longer meets the emergency 
engine requirements, the specific circumstances are required to be reported to Ohio EPA for 
evaluation and may require modifying the existing permit or submitting a new permit application. 
Comment 51: Is the potential to emit based on 100 hours of operation? 
Response 51: The potential to emit is based on 500 hours of operation per year. This approach 
follows the U.S. EPA memorandum "Calculating Potential to Emit (PTE) for Emergency 
Generators" (Sept. 6, 1995). 
Comment 52: How many hours per year are the generators expected to be operated for testing and 
maintenance? 
Response 52: Based on operations at similar facilities in Ohio, testing and maintenance are typically 
no more than 12 hours per year per engine. 
Comment 53: Commenters asked how Ohio EPA can prove the use of Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil 
(HVO) as fuel is equivalent to the use of diesel from an environmental standpoint. 
Response 53: All available information on the use of HVO as a replacement fuel indicates that HVO 
is an extremely clean fuel and superior to diesel from an environmental standpoint. The company 
provided documentation from two different engine manufacturers stating their approval for the use 
of alternative diesel fuels, including HVO, in the engines. Once the final engine designs have bee

title: 4132514.pdf
text:
selected, Ohio EPA will verify with the manufacturer that HVO fuel can be used without 
any modifications to the engine. If the manufacturer does not approve the use of HVO as an 
alternative fuel, a permit modification would be required. 
Comment 54: What PM2.5 limits are established in the permit for the generators? 
Response 54: No specific PM2.5 limit is established in the permit. The particulate limit for the engines 
is established under 40 CFR Part 60 Subpart IIII, with a performance standard of 0.20 grams PM/kW-
hr, which effectively restricts PM2,5. 
Comment 55: One commenter suggested that the permit restrict the maximum number of engines 
that can be operated at one time during routine testing, as they are described in the Tyler Fox 
Memorandum. The same commenter also suggested that Ohio EPA limit non-emergency operating 
hours to between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. Both were proposed to minimize impacts, with consideration of 
meteorological conditions that maximize air dispersion and thus limit ground-level concentrations 
of NO2 from the emergency engines. 
Response 55: There is no legal requirement to limit the number of engines that can be operated 
simultaneously during testing or to place restrictions on operations for the purpose of maximizing 
air dispersion. On a per-engine basis, NOx emissions from testing scenarios are substantially lower 
than when the engines are operating at full load. Ohio EPA can observe maintenance testing events 
and require further modeling to ensure that NOx emissions do not have a significant negative impact. 
Ohio EPA can require changes in scheduling if there are excessive impacts on ambient air quality. 
Comment 56: What are the emissions limits on low-sulfur diesel fuel and HVO? 
Response 56: The ultra-low sulfur diesel and HVO fuel is required to meet a maximum sulfur 
concentration of 15 ppm (0.0015% sulfur by weight) and either a minimum cetane index of 40 or a 
maximum aromatic content of 35 volume percent. The engines are also required to meet the 
following standards: 0.20 grams PM/kW-hr, 6.4 grams NOx + NMHC/kW-hr, and 3.5 grams CO/kW-
hr. 
Topic: Water Use and Wastewater 
Comment 57: Commenters express concern about the environmental impact of the proposed 
facility's water use. They write that the facility, along with existing industries, may consume more 
water than the watershed can replenish. Commenters indicated construction activities have 
impacted private drinking water wells. 
Response 57: Impacts to private drinking water wells are managed by Ohio Department of Health 
and the local health department. Water withdrawal concerns are managed by Ohio Department of 
Natural Resources (ODNR). 
Comment 58: Commenters had several concerns about wastewater discharges from the facility. 
How will Ohio EPA monitor for Legionella or other pathogens in the cooling water discharge? Where 
and how is this wastewater going to be removed from this facility? Commenters also express concern 
that wastewater will worsen local water quality. They note that water permit issues have not 
received the same public attention as air permits. 
Response 58: If a data center does not send its wastewater to a sanitary sewer, an Ohio EPA 
wastewater discharge permit (also called a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System, or 
NPDES) may be required for cooling-water blowdown discharges. If sewer service is unavailable or 
insufficient, an NPDES permit may authorize the data center to discharge to a nearby stream. This 
wastewater discharge permit requires routine monitoring and may require cooling ponds or other 
treatment to address issues such as water temperature or total dissolved solids.

title: 4132514.pdf
text:
Data centers using air-based or closed-loop cooling may still generate liquid waste that must be 
managed appropriately. 
Potential water quality impacts are not in the scope of the air permit. 
Topic: Power Grid 
Comment 59: Commenters worry that the facility's electricity demand could strain an already 
stressed power grid, potentially contributing to higher residential electric bills, rolling blackouts, or 
increased reliance on diesel generators. Others argue that the region's infrastructure is not prepared 
for the added load and that more research is needed before any permit is approved. 
Response 59: Ohio EPA is not involved in decisions on power infrastructure needs. Residents should 
contact their local electric provider or the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio. 
Topic: Wildlife, Animals, Agriculture, and Ecosystems 
Comment 60: Commenters are concerned about the proposed data center's impacts on ecosystems, 
watersheds, wildlife, and farmland. They are concerned about air emissions from cooling towers and 
power sources impacting livestock and depositing on farm crops. The comments also focus on 
stormwater runoff and wastewater impacting the watershed and soil quality. 
Response 60: To ensure wildlife is not impacted, Ohio EPA consults with ODNR and other agencies 
when drafting a permit that would affect waters of the state. The agency does not anticipate that the 
facility's air emissions will impact wildlife, agriculture, or ecosystems. 
Ohio EPA Division of Surface Water administers the Construction Stormwater Program under the 
federal Clean Water Act. Construction sites disturbing one acre or more must obtain coverage. 
Facility owners must also prepare a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan, submit a Notice of Intent, 
and receive Ohio EPA approval before starting work. 
Some data center projects may impact streams, wetlands, or lakes. Under Clean Water Act Sections 
401/404, any activity placing dredged or fill material into waters of the U.S. requires state and federal 
review and permitting. 
Currently, Ohio EPA has issued Bistrozzi an NPDES General Permit for Construction Stormwater 
issued to Turner Construction on Nov. 10, 2025 - 2GC08468. Bistrozzi (Project BOSC) applied for and 
later withdrew an application for impacts to a level 2 isolated wetland. After withdrawing that 
application, they applied for and were issued a level 1 isolated wetland permit. 
Topic: Noise 
Comment 61: Commenters express concern about noise from the facility, which would diminish 
quality of life, limit outdoor activities, disrupt sleep, and cause stress, noise sensitivity, and tinnitus. 
Commenters express concern that the noise would not comply with local ordinances and ask whether 
any formal noise-impact studies would be conducted. 
Response 61: While we understand that noise is a concern at facilities, it is outside of Ohio EPA's 
permitting authority. Often, local municipalities have noise ordinances. For noise concerns or 
questions, please reach out to American Township. 
Topic: Grave Site 
Comment 62: One commenter indicated that there is a burial site on the property. The commenter 
requested information about the site's future. 
Response 62: Ohio EPA requested the company to contact the commenter directly to address this 
concern. 
Topic: Additional Comments Unrelated to Air Permit

title: 4132514.pdf
text:
Comment 63: Commenters expressed concern for topics unrelated to the proposed air permit, such 
as local drought conditions, flooding, zoning issues, property values, better venues for public 
meetings, construction activities, and a lack of trust in officials and the permitting process. Some 
residents request participation from people who have published articles about data centers. Overall, 
the submissions reflect significant apprehension with the proposed facility. 
Response 63:These concerns are outside of Ohio EPA's permitting authority. We understand how 
important these issues are to the local community and encourage residents to engage with their local 
municipalities and county resources to address them. 
Regarding comments about the public meeting location for the draft air permit, Ohio EPA typically 
seeks a hearing location as close as possible to the proposed facility site and one that accommodates 
the anticipated crowd. We underestimated attendance for this hearing based on public inquiries to 
Ohio EPA. To ensure the community had enough time to submit comments or concerns about the 
draft permit, Ohio EPA provided a 48-day comment period, which is two additional weeks beyond 
what is required. 
Topic: General Comments Against the Project 
Comment 64: Many residents oppose the proposed data center, citing concerns about its 
environmental, economic, and quality-of-life impacts. Many believe the facility would strain local 
water resources, reduce farmland, raise household utility costs, harm property values, and threaten 
local wildlife habitats. Others link their concerns to broader skepticism about data centers, artificial 
intelligence systems, and data security. Several note that similar facilities create few permanent jobs, 
raising doubts about economic benefits, especially with extended tax abatements and increased 
infrastructure demands. 
Response 64: While we appreciate community feedback, Ohio EPA must issue permits that comply 
with Ohio's environmental laws and regulations. The draft air permit does meet those requirements. 
We cannot deny a permit based on local popularity for the facility or business sector. 
End of Response to Comments

Good morning, Catherine, 
 
This notification is provided to you in accordance with the Consultation Protocol Among the United 
States Army Corps of Engineers Buffalo, Huntington, Louisville, Pittsburgh Districts Regulatory Offices 
and the Ohio SHPO Regarding Implementation of the Regulatory Program within the State of Ohio dated 
April 2025. 
 
I refer to the Department of the Army (DA) permit application submitted by 68 Yards, LLC, and received in 
this office on 1 December 2025, with additional information received on 19 December 2025, and 29 
January 2026.  The applicant, 68 Yards, LLC, has requested authorization under the United States Army 
Corps of Engineers (Corps) Nationwide Permit (NWP) 39 for the discharge of dredged and/or fill material 
into waters of the United States associated with the Buck Canyon Site Project.  The proposed Buck 
Canyon Site Project encompasses approximately 1,016 acres located north and east of Ginger Ridge 
Road and west of U.S. Route 52 in Manchester, Sprigg Township, Adams County, Ohio at approximately 
38.646748 latitude, -83.659828 longitude The proposed project occurs within the Crooked Creek-Ohio 
River and Lawrence Creek-Ohio River watersheds, 12-digit Hydrologic Unit Codes 050902010601 and 
050902010605, respectively. The proposed project area can be found on the United States Geological 
Survey (USGS) Maysville East, Ohio 1:24K quadrangle topographic map.  On-site waters include and flow 
to Elk Run, a tributary of the Ohio River. The Ohio River is traditional navigable water of the United States. 
The following file number has been assigned to this proposed project: LRH-2025-00457-OHR-Elk Run.  
 
The proposed project would involve construction of an industrial development including twelve (12) 
buildings, internal roadways, five (5) stormwater management basins, and utility infrastructure. The 
proposed project would result in the permanent discharge of dredged and/or fill material into 1,893 
linear feet (0.364 acre) of four (4) streams (Stream 9 – 258 linear feet [0.017 acre], Stream 24 – 847 linear 
feet [0.098 acre], Elk Run – 303 linear feet [0.12 acre], and Carter Hollow – 485 linear feet [0.129 acre]) for 
grading, filling, and culvert installation. Additionally, the proposed project would involve the permanent 
discharge of dredged and/or fill material into 0.06 acre of two (2) wetlands (Wetland E – 0.01 acre and 
Wetland G – 0.05 acre) for grading and filling. All work, avoidance, and minimization measures would be 
conducted as outlined in the pre-construction notification (PCN) received in our office on 1 December 
2025, and additional information received 19 December 2025, and 29 January 2026. The applicant has 
proposed to utilize best management practices (BMPs) and implement a site-specific Stormwater 
Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) to minimize indirect effects to aquatic resources. 
 
On behalf the applicant, R. Christopher Goodwin & Associates, Inc., coordinated with the survey 
approach, methods, and results with the Ohio State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) in December of 
2025. R. Christopher Goodwin & Associates, Inc. conducted a Cultural Resources Desktop Review of the

title: Email Chain 11.pdf
text:
2
proposed project area, a Phase I Architectural Reconnaissance Survey, and Phase Ib Archaeological and 
Phase II Archaeological Surveys for the proposed project.  
 
A Phase I Architectural Survey for the Proposed Buck Canyon Project, Adams County, Ohio, was 
conducted in April and May of 2025 by with the primary goal being to evaluate aboveground resources 
over 45 years of age within the LOD and within 0.5 mile (0.8 kilometer) of the direct APE. The Phase I 
Architectural Reconnaissance Survey revealed 33 properties older than 45 years within the direct and 
indirect APE. 
 
In a response letter dated 13 January 2026 the Ohio SHPO stated: 
 
Twenty-one (21) of the properties were recommended as not eligible for listing in the National 
Register of Historic Places (NRHP). The locations of five (5) previously surveyed properties could 
not be verified, and six (6) properties were inaccessible from the public right-of-way to be 
evaluated. In addition, the Showboat Majestic (Ref. No. 80003085) has been moved from its 
documented spot and is potentially in Greenup, Kentucky. Two (2) of the surveyed properties are 
located within or immediately adjacent to the Project Area. The Boone Family Cemetery at 1669 
Ginger Ridge Road is recommended to have visual screening added on the Project Area, and the 
Rogers Parr Cemetery was surveyed as part of the archaeology investigation. The recommended 
avoidance to this cemetery will be based on the archaeology recommendations. However, the 
SHPO agrees with all other recommendations for the above ground resources. 
 
The Corps concurs with Ohio SHPO’s eligibility determinations for the aboveground resources identified 
during the Phase I Architectural Reconnaissance Survey and has determined the proposed project would 
have no effect on NRHP-eligible of NRHP-listed historic architectural resources.  
 
R. Christopher Goodwin & Associates, Inc. completed Phase IB Archaeological Survey and Phase II 
Evaluations of Sites 33AD399, 33AD404, and 33AD405 for the Proposed Buck Canyon Project, Adams 
County, Ohio in August 2025. The limits of disturbance (LOD) for the proposed industrial project 
encompasses approximately 1,009 acres; however, approximately 770 acres were previously surveyed 
(Purtill, Norr, and Owen 2008). The Phase I investigations included a literature review, visual inspection, 
and shovel test unit excavations of approximately 251 acres, which identified three (3) new Ohio 
Archaeological Inventory (OAI) sites (33AD0477-33AD0479) and expanded four (4) previously 
documented sites (33AD0393, 33AD0395, 33AD0401, and 33AD0402). The Phase II investigations 
incorporated a literature review, visual inspection,1-x-1-m and 1-x-2-m test units, and shovel test unit 
excavations at three (3) previously documented sites (33AD0399, 33AD0404, and 33AD0405). 
 
In a response letter dated 13 January 2026 the Ohio SHPO stated: 
 
Sites 33AD0393, 33AD0395, 33AD0401, and 33AD0402 were expanded during the Phase I survey 
based on the presence of additional surface features; however, the sites contained disturbed 
contexts and yielded few artifacts. Our office agrees that these sites are not eligible for the NRHP; 
no additional survey is recommended. 
 
Sites 33AD0477 and 33AD0478 had been previously disturbed by demolition, while 33AD0479 
contained two (2) artifacts. Our office agrees that these sites are not eligible for the NRHP; no 
additional survey is recommended.

title: Email Chain 11.pdf
text:
3
The previously unrecorded Davidson Cemetery was documented within the expanded boundaries 
of 33AD0401. It has since been recorded on the Ohio Historic Inventory (OHI; ADA0063512). It has 
been recommended for avoidance in accordance with our office’s Archaeology Guidelines, which 
recommend a minimum 100-foot-wide construction buffer around the known extent of the 
cemetery (SHPO 2022). 
 
The Phase II evaluations documented extensive disturbance from grading, filling, and demolition 
at 33AD0399; however, the Rogers Parr Cemetery was largely intact. It is Goodwin & Associates’ 
recommendation that the Rogers Cemetery should be avoided by all construction activities. 
 
The evaluations of 33AD0404 and 33AD0405 yielded artifacts consistent with the more recent 
twentieth-century occupations of both sites. It is Goodwin & Associates’ recommendations that 
these sites lack the integrity and research potential necessary for inclusion on the NRHP. Our 
office agrees with the recommendations. 
 
The Boone Cemetery (OGS ID 85, which has also been recorded as the Little #1 Cemetery (OGS ID 
13191), is located along Ginger Ridge Road and immediately adjacent to the LOD. Due to its 
proximity to the LOD, our office recommends a minimum 100-foot-wide buffer from construction 
activities at the Boone Cemetery, in addition to the recommended visual screening. 
 
In summary, our office agrees with the recommendations of eligibility for the above ground and 
archaeological resources evaluated through these investigations. Additionally, we recommend 
avoidance for the Boone Cemetery, Rogers Parr Cemetery, and Davidson Cemetery. Our office’s 
2022 Archaeology Guidelines recommends a minimum 100-foot-wide buffer from construction 
activities around the furthest known extent of any cemetery. We also request that the buffer be 
depicted on any project construction plans and delineated by temporary fencing before and 
during construction. 
 
The Corps concurs with Ohio SHPO’s NRHP-eligibility determinations and agrees that Sites 33AD0393, 
33AD0395, 33AD0401, 33AD0402, 33AD0477, 33AD0478, 33AD0479, 33AD0404, and 33AD0405 are not 
eligible for listing in the NRHP under Criterion A, B, C, or D. 
 
Based on the 100-foot avoidance buffer recommended by Ohio SHPO’s guidelines around the known 
boundaries The Boone Cemetery (OGS ID 85, which has also been recorded as the Little #1 Cemetery 
(OGS ID 13191), Rogers Parr Cemetery, and Davidson Cemetery (OHI ADA0063512), a meeting was held 
on 16 January 2026, between the Corps, the applicant, the Ohio SHPO, and the applicant’s agent, R. 
Christopher Goodwin & Associates, Inc, to discuss the cemetery avoidance plan. During the discussion 
it was determined that a 100-foot buffer and existing vegetation around the known boundaries of the 
three (3) cemeteries would be maintained, temporary construction fencing would be installed at the 100-
foot buffer around the Boone Family Cemetery and the Davidson Cemetery Cemetery during 
construction activities. Due to proximity of the proposed development to the Rogers Parr Cemetery, 
permanent fencing would be installed along the perimeter of the 100-foot cemetery buffer. Furthermore, 
temporary signage would be installed near the Boone Cemetery, Davidson Family Cemetery, and Rogers 
Parr Cemetery to allow access. Post construction, pedestrian access would be maintained to the three 
(3) cemetery resources. 
 
As requested by the Corps and the Ohio SHPO, the applicant provided a design plan depicting the 100-
foot buffer around the Boone Cemetery (OGS ID 85, which has also been recorded as the Little #1

title: Email Chain 11.pdf
text:
4
Cemetery (OGS ID 13191), Rogers Parr Cemetery, and Davidson Cemetery (OHI ADA0063512) on 29 
January 2026. In addition to the design plan submission, the avoidance plan stipulates the 
aforementioned temporary construction fencing around the Boone Family Cemetery and the Davidson 
Cemetery, the permanent fencing along the perimeter of the 100-foot buffer from the Rogers Parr 
Cemetery, as well as the temporary signage for access during construction and post construction.  
 
Based on the avoidance measures provided for the Boone Cemetery (OGS ID 85, which has also been 
recorded as the Little #1 Cemetery (OGS ID 13191), Rogers Parr Cemetery, and Davidson Cemetery (OHI 
ADA0063512), the Corps has determined the proposed project would not affect these cemetery 
resources. The following special conditions would be added to any permit verification to ensure 
compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. 
 
Special Condition 1: To ensure compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation 
Act and to avoid inadvertent impacts to known cemetery resources, the applicant shall install high-
visibility temporary construction fencing around the 100-foot buffer of the known boundaries of the 
Boone Cemetery and the Davidson Cemetery during construction activities, as well as maintain 
existing vegetative buffers within the 100-foot buffer. Permanent fencing will be installed along the 
100-foot buffer perimeter around the known boundary of the Rogers Parr Cemetery prior to 
construction. The applicant shall install temporary signage during construction, providing a point of 
contact to afford access to the three (3) cemeteries during construction. Pedestrian access to the 
cemeteries will be maintained following project construction. 
 
Special Condition 2: In the event any previously unknown historic or archaeological sites or human 
remains are uncovered while accomplishing the activity authorized by this nationwide permit 
authorization, the permittee must cease all work in waters of the United States immediately and 
contact local, state and county law enforcement offices (only contact law enforcement on findings 
of human remains), the Corps at 304-399-5210 and Ohio State Historic Preservation Office at 614-
298-2000.  The Corps will initiate the Federal, state and tribal coordination required to comply with 
the National Historic Preservation Act and applicable state and local laws and 
regulations.  Federally recognized tribes are afforded a government-to-government status as 
sovereign nations and consultation is required under Executive Order 13175 and 36 CFR Part 800. 
 
The Corps has reviewed the project plans associated with the Buck Canyon Site Development Project 
and the Ohio SHPO’s letter of concurrence regarding the NRHP eligibly of the impacted resources. The 
Corps concurs with the no effect on historic properties determination made by the Ohio SHPO for the 
proposed project based on the cemetery avoidance plan provided by the applicant.  
 
The Corps concurs with the Ohio SHPO’s no effect to historic properties determination.  Therefore, in 
accordance with 36 CFR § 800.4(d)(1), it has been determined no historic properties would be affected 
by the proposed undertaking.  The Corps considers the documentation satisfactory to fulfill its SHPO 
consultation responsibilities under Section 106 of the NHPA and its own regulations (33 CFR Parts 320-
332, including Appendix C of 33 CFR Part 325 while valid and applicable).  Tribal coordination will not be 
required for the proposed undertaking.   
 
Please let me know if you have any questions.  
 
Thank you,  
Lee

Survey (USGS) Maysville East, Ohio 1:24K quadrangle topographic map.  On-site waters include and flow 
to Elk Run, a tributary of the Ohio River. The Ohio River is traditional navigable water of the United States. 
The following file number has been assigned to this proposed project: LRH-2025-00457-OHR-Elk Run.  
  
The proposed project would involve construction of an industrial development including twelve (12) 
buildings, internal roadways, five (5) stormwater management basins, and utility infrastructure. The 
proposed project would result in the permanent discharge of dredged and/or fill material into 1,893 
linear feet (0.364 acre) of four (4) streams (Stream 9 – 258 linear feet [0.017 acre], Stream 24 – 847 linear 
feet [0.098 acre], Elk Run – 303 linear feet [0.12 acre], and Carter Hollow – 485 linear feet [0.129 acre]) for 
grading, filling, and culvert installation. Additionally, the proposed project would involve the permanent 
discharge of dredged and/or fill material into 0.06 acre of two (2) wetlands (Wetland E – 0.01 acre and 
Wetland G – 0.05 acre) for grading and filling. All work, avoidance, and minimization measures would be 
conducted as outlined in the pre-construction notification (PCN) received in our office on 1 December 
2025, and additional information received 19 December 2025, and 29 January 2026. The applicant has 
proposed to utilize best management practices (BMPs) and implement a site-specific Stormwater 
Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) to minimize indirect effects to aquatic resources. 
  
On behalf the applicant, R. Christopher Goodwin & Associates, Inc., coordinated with the survey 
approach, methods, and results with the Ohio State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) in December of 
2025. R. Christopher Goodwin & Associates, Inc. conducted a Cultural Resources Desktop Review of the 
proposed project area, a Phase I Architectural Reconnaissance Survey, and Phase Ib Archaeological and 
Phase II Archaeological Surveys for the proposed project.  
  
A Phase I Architectural Survey for the Proposed Buck Canyon Project, Adams County, Ohio, was 
conducted in April and May of 2025 by with the primary goal being to evaluate aboveground resources 
over 45 years of age within the LOD and within 0.5 mile (0.8 kilometer) of the direct APE. The Phase I 
Architectural Reconnaissance Survey revealed 33 properties older than 45 years within the direct and 
indirect APE. 
  
In a response letter dated 13 January 2026 the Ohio SHPO stated: 
  
Twenty-one (21) of the properties were recommended as not eligible for listing in the National 
Register of Historic Places (NRHP). The locations of five (5) previously surveyed properties could 
not be verified, and six (6) properties were inaccessible from the public right-of-way to be 
evaluated. In addition, the Showboat Majestic (Ref. No. 80003085) has been moved from its 
documented spot and is potentially in Greenup, Kentucky. Two (2) of the surveyed properties are 
located within or immediately adjacent to the Project Area. The Boone Family Cemetery at 1669 
Ginger Ridge Road is recommended to have visual screening added on the Project Area, and the 
Rogers Parr Cemetery was surveyed as part of the archaeology investigation. The recommended 
avoidance to this cemetery will be based on the archaeology recommendations. However, the 
SHPO agrees with all other recommendations for the above ground resources. 
  
The Corps concurs with Ohio SHPO’s eligibility determinations for the aboveground resources identified 
during the Phase I Architectural Reconnaissance Survey and has determined the proposed project would 
have no effect on NRHP-eligible of NRHP-listed historic arc

R. Christopher Goodwin & Associates, Inc. completed Phase IB Archaeological Survey and Phase II 
Evaluations of Sites 33AD399, 33AD404, and 33AD405 for the Proposed Buck Canyon Project, Adams 
County, Ohio in August 2025. The limits of disturbance (LOD) for the proposed industrial project 
encompasses approximately 1,009 acres; however, approximately 770 acres were previously surveyed 
(Purtill, Norr, and Owen 2008). The Phase I investigations included a literature review, visual inspection, 
and shovel test unit excavations of approximately 251 acres, which identified three (3) new Ohio 
Archaeological Inventory (OAI) sites (33AD0477-33AD0479) and expanded four (4) previously 
documented sites (33AD0393, 33AD0395, 33AD0401, and 33AD0402). The Phase II investigations 
incorporated a literature review, visual inspection,1-x-1-m and 1-x-2-m test units, and shovel test unit 
excavations at three (3) previously documented sites (33AD0399, 33AD0404, and 33AD0405). 
  
In a response letter dated 13 January 2026 the Ohio SHPO stated: 
  
Sites 33AD0393, 33AD0395, 33AD0401, and 33AD0402 were expanded during the Phase I survey 
based on the presence of additional surface features; however, the sites contained disturbed 
contexts and yielded few artifacts. Our office agrees that these sites are not eligible for the NRHP; 
no additional survey is recommended. 
  
Sites 33AD0477 and 33AD0478 had been previously disturbed by demolition, while 33AD0479 
contained two (2) artifacts. Our office agrees that these sites are not eligible for the NRHP; no 
additional survey is recommended. 
  
The previously unrecorded Davidson Cemetery was documented within the expanded boundaries 
of 33AD0401. It has since been recorded on the Ohio Historic Inventory (OHI; ADA0063512). It has 
been recommended for avoidance in accordance with our office’s Archaeology Guidelines, which 
recommend a minimum 100-foot-wide construction buffer around the known extent of the 
cemetery (SHPO 2022). 
  
The Phase II evaluations documented extensive disturbance from grading, filling, and demolition 
at 33AD0399; however, the Rogers Parr Cemetery was largely intact. It is Goodwin & Associates’ 
recommendation that the Rogers Cemetery should be avoided by all construction activities. 
  
The evaluations of 33AD0404 and 33AD0405 yielded artifacts consistent with the more recent 
twentieth-century occupations of both sites. It is Goodwin & Associates’ recommendations that 
these sites lack the integrity and research potential necessary for inclusion on the NRHP. Our 
office agrees with the recommendations. 
  
The Boone Cemetery (OGS ID 85, which has also been recorded as the Little #1 Cemetery (OGS ID 
13191), is located along Ginger Ridge Road and immediately adjacent to the LOD. Due to its 
proximity to the LOD, our office recommends a minimum 100-foot-wide buffer from construction 
activities at the Boone Cemetery, in addition to the recommended visual screening. 
  
In summary, our office agrees with the recommendations of eligibility for the above ground and 
archaeological resources evaluated through these investigations. Additionally, we recommend 
avoidance for the Boone Cemetery, Rogers Parr Cemetery, and Davidson Cemetery. Our office’s 
2022 Archaeology Guidelines recommends a minimum 100-foot-wide buffer from construction 
activities around the furthest known extent of any cemetery. We also request that the buffer be

depicted on any project construction plans and delineated by temporary fencing before and 
during construction. 
  
The Corps concurs with Ohio SHPO’s NRHP-eligibility determinations and agrees that Sites 33AD0393, 
33AD0395, 33AD0401, 33AD0402, 33AD0477, 33AD0478, 33AD0479, 33AD0404, and 33AD0405 are not 
eligible for listing in the NRHP under Criterion A, B, C, or D. 
  
Based on the 100-foot avoidance buffer recommended by Ohio SHPO’s guidelines around the known 
boundaries The Boone Cemetery (OGS ID 85, which has also been recorded as the Little #1 Cemetery 
(OGS ID 13191), Rogers Parr Cemetery, and Davidson Cemetery (OHI ADA0063512), a meeting was held 
on 16 January 2026, between the Corps, the applicant, the Ohio SHPO, and the applicant’s agent, R. 
Christopher Goodwin & Associates, Inc, to discuss the cemetery avoidance plan. During the discussion 
it was determined that a 100-foot buffer and existing vegetation around the known boundaries of the 
three (3) cemeteries would be maintained, temporary construction fencing would be installed at the 100-
foot buffer around the Boone Family Cemetery and the Davidson Cemetery Cemetery during 
construction activities. Due to proximity of the proposed development to the Rogers Parr Cemetery, 
permanent fencing would be installed along the perimeter of the 100-foot cemetery buffer. Furthermore, 
temporary signage would be installed near the Boone Cemetery, Davidson Family Cemetery, and Rogers 
Parr Cemetery to allow access. Post construction, pedestrian access would be maintained to the three 
(3) cemetery resources. 
  
As requested by the Corps and the Ohio SHPO, the applicant provided a design plan depicting the 100-
foot buffer around the Boone Cemetery (OGS ID 85, which has also been recorded as the Little #1 
Cemetery (OGS ID 13191), Rogers Parr Cemetery, and Davidson Cemetery (OHI ADA0063512) on 29 
January 2026. In addition to the design plan submission, the avoidance plan stipulates the 
aforementioned temporary construction fencing around the Boone Family Cemetery and the Davidson 
Cemetery, the permanent fencing along the perimeter of the 100-foot buffer from the Rogers Parr 
Cemetery, as well as the temporary signage for access during construction and post construction.  
  
Based on the avoidance measures provided for the Boone Cemetery (OGS ID 85, which has also been 
recorded as the Little #1 Cemetery (OGS ID 13191), Rogers Parr Cemetery, and Davidson Cemetery (OHI 
ADA0063512), the Corps has determined the proposed project would not affect these cemetery 
resources. The following special conditions would be added to any permit verification to ensure 
compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. 
  
Special Condition 1: To ensure compliance with Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation 
Act and to avoid inadvertent impacts to known cemetery resources, the applicant shall install high-
visibility temporary construction fencing around the 100-foot buffer of the known boundaries of the 
Boone Cemetery and the Davidson Cemetery during construction activities, as well as maintain 
existing vegetative buffers within the 100-foot buffer. Permanent fencing will be installed along the 
100-foot buffer perimeter around the known boundary of the Rogers Parr Cemetery prior to 
construction. The applicant shall install temporary signage during construction, providing a point of 
contact to afford access to the three (3) cemeteries during construction. Pedestrian access to the 
cemeteries will be maintained following project construction. 
  
Special Condition 2: In the event any previously unknown historic or archaeological sites or human 
remains are uncovered while accomplishing the activity authorized by this nationwide permit 
authorization, the permittee must cease all work in waters of the United States immediately and

title: 5.4.26-Public-Hearing-1.pdf
text:
Esteemed Council Members and Dearest Citizens of Van Wert County, 
I write this letter as a former resident of Convoy, OH and as someone who has family, friends, former 
teachers, and former co-workers in the area. The facts, considerations, and notes I include in this letter 
are based not just on the sources I provide, but the knowledge I have gained in my Master of Science in 
Environmental Studies at Ohio University and my certificate in Appalachian Health, which focused on the 
health disparities that plague rural regions such as ours. These concerns and recommendations are 
further informed by my research experience with phytoremediation and the abatement of acid mine 
drainage. 
In no way am I strictly against data centers nor development; I have taught Digital Art and Technology at 
Ohio University where we trained our own supercomputer with non-copyrighted material. I understand the 
limitations and opportunities of this software, and understand that long before AI existed, data centers 
were powering our servers. Still, even the greatest proponent of AI would have every right to question how 
a data center would impact their community. One way to conceptualize these impacts is through 
watershed health. 
Over 243,000 people rely on the Auglaize watershed, as it’s shared between Convoy, Liberty, 
Wapakoneta, Lima, Spencerville, Delphos, Ohio City, Monroeville, Paulding, Continental and, of course, 
Van Wert (Ohio Watershed Data, 2021). Rain in Monroeville and Paulding recharges the wells  in Convoy. 
Likewise, pollution in Liberty impacts water quality in the Van Wert reservoir. Throughout any given year, a 
water system will experience low and high flow events. In a low flow period, when the depth of water is 
lessened, ephemeral ponds dry up, pollution becomes more concentrated, and waterbodies become 
warmer (Satzinger & Bachmann, 2025). While fluctuations are normal, external pressures can exasperate 
these effects and result in reduced ecosystem services, thereby negatively impacting human health 
(USDA, 2002).  
Watershed health is determined according to its safety for human and animal consumption as well as its 
ability to support aquatic life. The Auglaize watershed scored a C- for these factors in 2018 (University of 
Maryland Center for Environmental Science, 2018). If we zoom in more, and look at our subwatersheds, 
all subwatersheds in Van Wert County are impaired. Van Wert’s Lower Town Creek is impaired due to the 
presence of E. coli and polychlorinated biphenyls. As a result, our local water has not been able to support 
recreational use nor fish for human consumption since 2018 and, eight years since first detection, there is 
still no plan in place to address it (Environmental Protection Agency, 2026).   
There seems to be a misconception that a closed loop system means no water is lost. The term closed 
loop refers to the primary cooling loop, where water is used for cooling on one end and left to cool on the 
other. These systems are not leak-free, but they do use approximately 50-70% less water than traditional 
water-cooling systems by using enclosed systems, where water is not exposed to air (World Economic 
Forum, 2024). So, if the initial filling is 5,500 gallons, and a non-closed loop system would need to 
replenish that daily, we can calculate that the data center would need 2,500-1,650 gallons of water a day 
(Van Wert Ohio Data Center, 2026). Since this water will not be drawn from municipal supplies or wells, it 
must be coming directly from our surface water. Surface water supplies groundwater, so claiming that 
this data center will not draw from wells or municipal supplies, while technically true, is misleading. This 
will impact the available water in residents’ wells, as the data center will take the water before it has a 
chance to infiltrate our soil. In a comprehensive study on global industry attitudes, it was found that 
approximately 53% of data center operators do not track th

title: 5.4.26-Public-Hearing-1.pdf
text:
Study Institute, 2026). PFAS are the class of chemicals that DuPont knowingly poisoned the Ohio river 
with from the 1950s to 2013, whose intentional concealment of the health impacts were only discovered 
because a farmer in West Virginia noticed his cattle were dying (Ohio Attorney General, 2018). These 
chemicals are known carcinogens, decrease fertility in women, lead to developmental delays in children, 
suppress the immune system, and increase cholesterol levels (EPA, 2026). Traditional drinking water 
treatment technologies are not able to remove PFAS, meaning specialized systems must be implemented 
in order to remove them from our drinking water (EPA, 2026). As is, federal regulation requires public 
water systems to complete initial monitoring and begin ongoing compliance monitoring by 2027. These 
systems will not be required to reduce PFAS levels until 2029 (Environmental Protection Agency, 2026).   
With this in mind, we must consider who will pay for these specialized systems. Before allotments are 
made, the council must be proactive and implement such systems. Otherwise, we will be knowingly 
exposing our community members to PFAS. As is, the Ohio EPA has drafted a General Permit 
Authorization for Discharges from Data Center Facilities that would loosen regulations on water discharge 
(Ohio EPA, 2026). This permit recognizes that, in granting this permit, our water quality would suffer. So, if 
we choose to have the data center shoulder its own burdens of pollution, then we must draft local law in 
accordance.   
The creation of electricity requires water as well, with natural gas power plants consuming 2,800 gallons 
per MWh (US Energy Information Administration, 2023). With the data center projected to use 500 MWh, 
that’s 1,400,000 gallons of water an hour (Van Wert Data Center, 2026). If this electricity is generated in 
Van Wert, OH, that will reduce the available surface water and thereby our groundwater supply. If this 
electricity is produced elsewhere, then we become responsible for the impacts on that area’s water 
supply.   
The capacity of Van Wert, OH’s reservoir is 1.01 billion gallons and, in a drought, could provide Van Wert 
City with water for 15-16 months. The refill of this reservoir depends on local stream flow, with the creek 
being able to provide between 180 million to 1.26 billion gallons of water in a calendar year (City of Van 
Wert, 2023). While data on the precise withdrawal from just the reservoir is not publicly available, the 
annual public surface water withdrawal in Van Wert County, OH is 1.002 billion gallons. With the reservoir 
capacity, county surface water use, predicted drought usage in mind, and the very real possibility of the 
local stream only providing 180 million gallons of water in a year, it becomes clear that, contrary to the 
council’s claim, there isn’t an explicit excess of water in the Van Wert county reservoir. 
In fact, in August of 2025, Ohio saw less than a tenth of an inch of rain with Van Wert being in extreme 
drought in early October (Ohio’s Country Journal, 2025). Ohio is infamous for its drastic weather changes, 
and any drought followed by a heavy downpour will result in increased runoff, reducing the recharge of 
groundwater despite precipitation. In Van Wert County, 124 farmers have formally committed to 
addressing these concerns and to improving the health of our watershed, through the implementation of 
the Best Management Practices under the H2Ohio program (Van Wert Soil & Water Conservation District). 
Yet, the council appears to not take this community’s concerns about the watershed seriously, as though 
these are a select few voices that can be ignored. 
It my sincerest hope that this failure to take the community’s concerns seriously is out of ignorance, rather 
than maliciousness. The residents of Van Wert elected each of you in good faith, so I implore you to 
consider a moratorium until full transparency can be provided and proper env

AMENDED BY-LAWS OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF
THE ADAMS COUNTY REGIONAL WATER DISTRICT
BYLAW 1: NAME
The name ofthe regionalwater districtshallbe the Adams County RegionalWater District,
hereinafterreferredtoas the "Regional District".
BYLAW 2: BOARD OF TRUSTEES AND TERM OF OFFICE
1. The Board of Trustees of this districtshall be composed as per the entriesof the Court for
the District,as filedwith the Clerk of the Court of Common Pleas ofAdams County, Ohio,
on January 10,1994 and December 18, 1997 under Case No. 930355.
2. The Board of Trustees shall consist of nine Board members each serving three-year
offsettingterms. At the firstorganizationalmeeting of the District,threeTrustees shallbe
appointed fora term of one year; three Trustees fora term oftwo years;and threeTrustees
fora term of threeyears. Reappointment of each term isrenewable followingthe expiration
of each term of office.
3. During the firstregular meeting of the fiscalyear the Board of Trustees shallelecta
president,vice-president,and secretary/treasurerfrom among themselves, each of whom
shall hold officeuntilthe next organizational meeting, unless sooner removed by death,
resignation,or forcause,in accordance with Section 5 of thisbylaw.
4. Ifthe officeof any Trustee becomes vacant by reason of death, resignation,or removal of
office,a nominating committee consistingof three appointed Trustees shallnominate a
successor forappointment. The nominee must be approved by two-thirdsof the Trustees.
5. Trustees may be removed from officein the manner provided by law for the removal of
public officials.
BYLAW 3: TERRITORY
The territoryof the Regional Districtshall be any unincorporated areas of Adams and Brown
Counties and any incorporatedareas of Adams County as ordered by the Courts of Common Pleas
Court having jurisdictionforsuch matters. Other contiguous areas willbe considered by the Board
for inclusion in the Regional Districtifdetermined to be for the common good of the Regional
District,as a whole.

title: Minutes  - April 26.pdf
text:
MINUTES 
Regular Meeting 
April 9, 2026 
 
 The Board of Trustees of the Adams County Regional Water District met on the 
above date for its regular monthly meeting with the following present:  Tony Staggs, Brent 
Crawford, Lynn Weeks, Luke Rhonemus, David Tatman, Gerald Gray, and Aaron Tolle.  Tim 
Grooms attended the latter part of the meeting.  Chris Baxla was absent.  Also attending 
were Johnny Hayslip, Judy Rogers, Melissa Semple, Nathan Crothers, Brett Grooms, Chris 
Hanson, Lee Conkel, and Attorney David Grimes.  Visitors attending were Brian and Tracy 
Hargis. 
 
 The meeting opened with prayer and the Pledge of Allegiance led by Brent Crawford. 
 
 Mr. Hargis addressed the Board concerning a water leak at his property.  He fixed the 
leak and received a fair leak adjustment before discovering the leak was actually the 
District’s responsibility as it was at the hanger.  He was satisfied with the leak adjustment 
but concerned that the leak adjustment insurance only covered one leak within a year’s 
time.  President Staggs apologized for the company leak and stated that the situation would 
be taken into consideration if there was a customer leak at the property within the stated 
year’s time. 
 
 Brent Crawford moved to dispense with the reading of the minutes and to accept 
them as presented.  Luke Rhonemus seconded the motion with all in favor. 
 
 The correspondence was reviewed including a notice of substantial completion for 
the ARPA Water Lines Project and an email stating Melissa Semple had received a grant for 
the registration fee for the ORWA EXPO at Columbus in May. 
 
 The Board reviewed the following monthly expenditures:

title: Minutes  - April 26.pdf
text:
Lynn Weeks moved to approve the following invoice: 
 
  Invoice #079 from Bennett & Williams for GIS services - $6,738.75 
 
Brent Crawford seconded the motion with all in favor. 
 
 In old business, Nathan Crothers informed the Board that the metal detector had 
actually cost $817.00 instead of the approved $752.00 and that the mini split heaters came 
in at $2,395.00 instead of the approved $1,695.00.  David Tatman moved to approve the 
additional funds needed, seconded by Lynn Weeks with all in favor. 
 
 Johnny Hayslip informed the Board that Resolution 26-14 authorizing the cleaning of 
Well #1 and Well #6 for $23,400.00 for both was actually the price of each well cleaning.  
The following resolution was adopted rescinding Resolution 26-14 and authorizing 
$46,800.00:

title: Minutes  - April 26.pdf
text:
Engineer’s Report #1 (CHA Consulting, Inc. – Lee Conkel) 
 
1.  WTP High Service Pump Project – He was still working with the approval agency  
      and waiting to hear if the last submittal was acceptable. 
 
2.  Ductile Iron Water Line Replacement Project – The WSRLA application was  
      submitted.  He will finish the preliminary layout for District employees to review. 
      He plans to bid the project in the fall. 
 
3.  WTP Filter Replacement Project  - The WSRLA application was submitted and  
      he should know something about the OPWC funds within the next month.  Funds      
      would be released in July.  He was working on the design and will get with District  
      personnel to go over the schedule, access, and work items.  The project does not  
                    require Ohio EPA approval, but it does require notification to ensure the District is  
      adhering to the original design. 
 
4.  Ginger Ridge Water Line – Plans have been submitted to the Ohio EPA for review. 
 
5.  Pumpkin Ridge Tank Rehab – The WSRLA application has been submitted.  He  
      will send in the bid documents to the Ohio EPA for review so the project can be   
      bid and the tank painted in the fall. 
 
6.  ARC Applications – ARC applications are due at the close of business on May 22.  
      He will submit an application for the Coon Hill Tank Rehab. 
 
Engineer’s Report #2 (Verdantas – Keith Doll – written report) 
 
1.  ACRWD Winchester Industrial Park Elevated Water Storage Tank – A progress  
      meeting is scheduled with Caldwell Tanks for April 15.  The contractor will start 
      mobilizing and construction staking the following week.  A meeting still needs to  
      be coordinated with the Village of Winchester to review a potential connection to 
      the village system including a contract, master meter location and layout, etc. 
 
2.  Water Line/Booster Station – The date of advertisement for bids will be in late  
       April. 
 
3.  ARPA Water Line Project – The contractor’s warranty period has begun.  He is 
      currently working on the project closeout documentation. 
 
In the manager’s report, Johnny Hayslip reported the following: 
 
1.  Women Helping Women had contacted the business office and asked if the 
      District would be willing to participate in the “Chalk the Walk” program to bring 
      awareness of violence against women issues.  The Board gave permission for 
      the business office parking lot to be used for this.

title: Minutes  - April 26.pdf
text:
2.  The District employees should be able to install the mixer in the Sunshine Ridge 
      tank for approximately $1,200.00.  
 
3.  The Ohio Rural Water Association Expo will be held in May.  The cost of hotel  
       rooms and registrations will be approximately $1,104.00 for him, Nathan  
       Crothers, and Melissa Semple to attend.  Luke Rhonemus moved to approve 
        this travel request and was seconded by Lynn Weeks with all in favor. 
 
4.   He had not received any quotes for divers to come in to inspect tank interiors. 
       He will try to obtain information at the Expo for this from other water companies. 
 
5.    If the Board wishes to have a fair booth again this year, he suggests a limit of 
        $2,000.00 in order to purchase additional brochures and materials. 
 
6.   The cost of a new Exmark lawnmower for the water treatment plant will cost 
       $16,489.00.  The repair of the old one would cost approximately  $6,800.00.   
       The Board needs to decide which avenue to pursue. 
 
7.   The Caterpillar bulldozer, which had been left at a work site for quite some time, 
       had been used by someone and became damaged.  A police report was issued.  
       The Board instructed District personnel to obtain an estimate on the repair of 
        it and then a decision will be made if the District’s insurance will be notified of 
        the situation. 
 
Nathan Crothers addressed the Board and requested that the money appropriated  
in the budget be released to purchase a ¾-ton service truck.  He has a quote from Barry’s 
Chevrolet for either a gas or diesel model.  He prefers the gas model as the diesel model 
does not do well idling with the strobe lights on the truck.  The budgeted amount for the 
truck chassis and bed is $79,000.00 and the truck accessories is allocated at $10,000.00. 
 
 Mr. Crothers also asked the Board to release the appropriated funding for the 
equipment garage that was allocated in the 2026 budget in the amount of $74,000.00. 
 
 The District’s dump truck has never been equipped with strobe lights and the lack 
could possibly be a safety issue.  It will cost approximately $1,400.00 to rectify the 
situation. 
 
 There are several pieces of equipment and miscellaneous inventory that have  
become obsolete or are no longer being used by the District.  The equipment includes a 
Kubota Mini U35 excavator, a 14,000 GVW Moritz trailer, a Rycom locator, a 185 Sullair air 
compressor, three air hogs, an Allis Chalmers forklift, two Exmark mowers, a 2011 Dodge 
Ram 2500 truck, and an eight-foot tilt trailer.  These could either be sold at auction or 
placed on the GovDeals website to sell.

title: Minutes  - April 26.pdf
text:
Chris Hanson addressed the Board about getting a PTZ (pan-tilt-zoom) camera for 
the well field.  He was checking prices and stated they range from $5,700.00 to $8,200.00. 
Trustee Tatman provided a name of a person the Western Brown School District uses for 
camera/camera installation to get another quote. 
 
 Mr. Hanson also stated that the gate opener at the water treatment plant was not 
working properly.  Johnny Hayslip will look into this to see what can be done. 
 
 Brett Grooms informed the Board that one of the endpoint cell transmitters had 
been installed at the Clayton Tank and they were still trying to get it to work with the 
Harmony meter reading system. 
 
 Judy Rogers reported that the District had received $3,411.48 from the Adams 
County Auditor for tax assessments for delinquent water bills put on property taxes. 
 
 Melissa Semple reported that Invoice Cloud would like to send one deposit file per 
day instead of multiple files.  In order to allow this, a new contract needs to be signed. 
 
 Ms. Semple also stated that the three-year leak insurance contract is due for 
renewal in July and the pemium rates will probably be increased due to the  amount of 
claims received in the three-year period. 
 
 The following resolutions were adopted by the Board approving the fair booth, the 
purchase of a lawnmower, the purchase of a service vehicle, the construction of an 
equipment garage, the purchase of strobe lights for the dump truck, the disposition of 
obsolete equipment and inventory, and the new Invoice Cloud agreement:

title: Minutes  - April 26.pdf
text:

title: Minutes -January 2024.pdf
text:
MINUTES 
Regular Meeting 
January 11, 2024 
 
 
 The Board of Trustees of the Adams County Regional Water District met on the above 
date for its regular monthly meeting with the following trustees present:  Tony Staggs, Brent 
Crawford, Lynn Weeks, Luke Rhonemus, Gerald Gray, Chris Baxla, Sam Cooper, and Aaron Tolle.  
Trustee Daniel Fristoe was absent.  Also attending were Rick Adamson, Judy Rogers, Quintin 
Baker, and Attorney David Grimes.  Visitors were Jenny and Emily Caldwell and Mary Jane 
Campbell. 
 
 The meeting opened with prayer and the Pledge of Allegiance led by Rick Adamson. 
 
 The following resolution was adopted reappointing three trustees:

title: Minutes -January 2024.pdf
text:
Attorney Grimes administered the oath of office to Tony Staggs and Luke Rhonemus. 
 
 The election of officers followed.  Brent Crawford moved to nominate Tony Staggs as 
president.  Luke Rhonemus seconded the motion with seven in favor and none opposed. 
 
 Nominations were opened for vice-president.  Chris Baxla moved to nominate Luke 
Rhonemus, seconded by Sam Cooper with six in favor and Trustee Rhonemus abstaining. 
 
 Luke Rhonemus nominated Aaron Tolle as secretary-treasurer.  Lynn Weeks seconded 
the motion with six in favor and Trustee Tolle abstaining. 
 
 The visitors were representing the Village of West Union and were concerned about the 
District’s plan to start charging $3.00 per reading provided in order for the villages and the 
Adams County Commissioners to issue sewer bills to customers.  After voicing their concerns, 
they were informed that the District thought it was a fair charge due to the cost of the water 
meters the District used and the labor involved in reading the meters and issuing the readings 
to them.  It was suggested that they could possibly add a surcharge to the sewer bills to cover 
the cost. 
 
 Gerald Gray moved to dispense with the reading of the minutes and to accept them as 
submitted.  Brent Crawford seconded the motion with all in favor. 
 
 The Board reviewed the following monthly expenditures:

title: Minutes -January 2024.pdf
text:
In old business, Quintin Baker informed the Board that CIC had received an easement 
from Larry Anderson on the Winchester Industrial Park Water Line.  CIC had paid for two taps 
for him, as well as disconnection charges, liquidated damage charges, and reconnection charges 
in the amount of $5,900.00. 
 
 In the absence of Lee Conkel, Rick Adamson reported the following for him: 
 
 1.  Winchester Industrial Park Water Line – With the receiving of one of the needed 
       easements, there are two more needed before he can finalize the route of the 
       water line. 
 
 2.  ARPA Funds Water Line Project – The materials for the project was awarded to  
      Buckeye State Pipe.  The advertising for the water line installation will be January 16  
      and January 23 with the bid opening on February 8 at 1:00 P .M.  The easements will    
      need to be completed with a certified map to that fact signed by Attorney Grimes.   
                  The WSRLA  loan agreement will also need to be signed by Attorney Grimes.  That will  
      sent to him next week for review. 
 
 3.  Clayton and Eckmansville Tank Rehabs – This project will be advertised also on  
       January 16 and January 23 with bid opening on February 8 at 10:00 A.M. 
 
 4.  Rigdon Road/Logans Lane Water Line – Lloyd’s Excavating still has a couple thousand 
      feet of restoration to complete and is waiting for dry weather to finish.

title: Minutes -January 2024.pdf
text:
Resolution 23-46 approved a change order for the Rigdon Road/Logans Lane Water Line 
Project in the amount of $23,530.00.  The change order actually came in at $17,860.00.  Chris 
Baxla moved to approve the change order for the lesser amount, seconded by Lynn Weeks with 
all in favor. 
 
 Luke Rhonemus moved to go into executive session for personnel issues and potential 
litigation.  Gerald Gray seconded the motion.  Upon roll call vote, the motion passed with seven 
in favor and none opposed. 
 
 Gerald Gray moved to go out of executive session and to resume the remainder of the 
meeting.  Sam Cooper seconded the motion with all in favor. 
 
 Because Barbie Francis has never had a first-year evaluation raise, Aaron Tolle moved to 
allow Ms. Francis to receive this raise in February, to be fair to her, even though the new pay 
scale is now in effect.  Sam Cooper seconded the motion with all in favor. 
 
 Sam Cooper moved to approve permission for Rick Adamson to sign a non-disclosure 
agreement for a company interested in purchasing and developing the former Stuart Generating 
Plant land.  Brent Crawford seconded the motion with all in favor.   
 
 Rick Adamson reported the following: 
 
 1.  The regularly scheduled meetings in April and July need to be changed due to 
       management vacations and the Adams County Fair.  The Board agreed to change the  
       April meeting from April 11 to April 4 and the July meeting from July 11 to July 18. 
 
 2.  The computer security protection system, Vipre Security Group,  is offering a three- 
       year contract for $3,080.00, saving the District money over annual contracts. 
 
 3.   Once again he can procure a practice exam training package for water licenses with  
        unlimited users at a cost of $1,000.00 for the year. 
 
 4.   The District can purchase hoses and adapters from Bain Enterprises for use with the 
        new Wachs valve maintenance trailer which may be beneficial in pumping out the 
        monitoring wells, as well as in daily operations of the District.  The cost of these  
        accessories is $1,567.65. 
 
 5.   Bennett & Williams has submitted yearly contracts for the GIS services for  
                     $30,000.00, asset management services for $15,000.00, and monitoring well 
         sampling (four quarters) in the amount of $130,460.00. 
 
 6.   The 2024 budget allocates $100,000.00 for the purchase of a small dump truck. 
        He would like the Board to approve releasing the funds so he can start searching 
        for the best deal.

title: Minutes -January 2024.pdf
text:
7.   The business office needs a new printer/copier for daily operations and to print 
        the monthly water bills.  The 2024 budget allows $6,000.00 for this purchase. 
 
 8.    If the Board wishes to hire a field operator to begin work in the spring, the  
        District needs to advertise soon as the hiring process takes quite a while.  Aaron 
        Tolle moved to go ahead and advertise, seconded by Sam Cooper with all in favor. 
 
 9.   Quad County Service & Repair will be in to repair and replace filters on the  
        generator at the water treatment plant and to repair the Cherry Fork Booster 
        generator.   The estimated cost of these repairs will be $1,434.62. 
 
 The following resolutions were adopted concerning the authorization of a three-year 
subscription for antivirus protection, the purchase of the online practice testing package,  
the purchase of accessories for the Wachs valve maintenance trailer, the approval of the three 
Bennett & Williams contracts, the purchase of a dump truck, and the purchase of a 
printer/copier for the business office:

title: Minutes -January 2024.pdf
text:
Quintin Baker reported that there were three Ohio EPA grants available on a first-come 
basis.  These grants consist of an Asset Management Program grant for $15,000.00, a Source 
Water Protection Strategies grant for $20,000.00, and a Well Abandonment grant for 
$15,000.00.  He will look into applying for each of these grants if the District qualifies according 
to the need for such grants.  As these are reimbursable grants, the District would have to pay in 
advance for the costs so he will get back to the Board should a grant be awarded. 
 
Sam Cooper moved to adjourn, seconded by Luke Rhonemus, with all in favor.

      President 
 
 
 
      __________________________________ 
      Secretary

Clerk of the Board

text:
Keith Doll,Verdantas engineer, informed management that the award date for the
funding for the Winchester IndustrialPark Water Line/Booster willnot be untilSeptember 24.
Should the Board wish to award the contracts for this project before this 98-day period, the
Districtwillhave to cover any pay requests untilthe funding isavailable. The pay requests
willbe refundable from the funding agency. Another alternative would be to ask B.P. Pipeline
foran extension before officiallyofferingthem the award document as the notice of award is
required within 90 days.
Johnny Hayslip stated that,forfuture expansion, a 12" stub with a valve and cap
could be installed on the south side of State Route 32 while the road bore is being installed
to serve the Winchester Industrial Park on the north sidefora cost of approximately $8,700
of inventory materials.
Judy Rogers stated that a laptop needs to be purchased for Melissa Semple to use as
the older computer she currently uses does not have enough memory. A new laptop can be
purchased forapproximately $2,000.00.
Melissa Semple informed the Board that the audit was currently underway. Itwas
suggested that an increase in the capital asset threshold be increased to $5,000.00 for
depreciable items.
Ms. Semple asked the Board ifthey wished to post a job opening for a water
plant operator. Chris Baxla moved to advertise for a Class IIor Class IIIWater Operator,
seconded by Brent Crawford with allinfavor.
The Board stated that the "Interim" could be removed from Johnny Hayslip's titleto
now become General Manager. His salary willbe discussed at a laterdate.
The Budget Committee presented the OfficialCertificate of Estimated Resources and
Expenditures for FiscalYear 2027.
Nathan Crothers informed the Board of the need of a hydraulic saw for use inthe
distributionsystem. He has a quote of $6,670.95 and would likethe Board's permission to
purchase the saw as long as itiscompatible with the District'sequipment.
The following resolutions were adopted concerning the authorization for the 12" stub
forfuture expansion, the purchase of a laptop, an increase inthe capitalizationthreshold,
the approving of the 2027 budget, the authorizing of a general engineering services contract,
the awarding of Contract 1 and Contract 2 for the Winchester IndustrialPark Project,and the
purchase of a hydraulic saw:
